en: *Ganshan Yunwo Jitan* (Records of Cloud-Reclining at Mount Gan):
Originally, I departed from Nanmin and returned far to Jiangbiao. I resolved to share my fate with the grasses and trees, clearing away the brambles on Chengshan to establish a hermitage.
There, I displayed the characters for "Yunwo An" (Cloud-Reclining Hermitage) inscribed by the late Minister Sun Gong Zhongyi. Furthermore, the Master...
I received a poem sent to me, which contained the lines: "Body and world are at odds; / Amidst the clouds, I lie still, not flying.
This clearly shows that he understands me. The mountain peak is high and cold, unsuitable for one of my age. As the eight seasons have passed, my ailments increase with each day.
Consequently, I moved my residence to Ganshan in Qujiang. As years advance, I grow increasingly distant from the world, simply following the flow of time.

One should act according to the circumstances to await the overflowing [of leisure]. Sometimes one may escape the fearsome heat in a pine grove; sometimes one may bask in the lovely sun beneath a thatched eaves.

With body at ease and free from affairs, when guests or friends happen to visit and there is no excuse to be made, one may then draw upon the public officials, veteran monks, and their bequeathed words or extraordinary traces as previously seen and heard, raising them up to serve as material for conversation beyond the mundane world.
Regarding the joy of this laughter: it is not that you, my friends, have not heard of it in passing, for your ears have long been familiar with it.

Thus, we have recorded it together and titled it *Yunwo Jitan* (Discourses from Cloud-Lying). However, what I have discussed here may not necessarily be considered excellent by the worthies of the world.
To have caused these to be gathered and compiled into a volume—is this not perhaps my own excessive fault?

As for the nature of words being empty and the path of speech being cut off, if I were to consider my lifelong discourse as never having been spoken at all, then I might approach that ideal. This is the self-narrative of the old monk Yunwoan.

*Ganshan Yunwo Jitan*, Volume One.
During the Xining era, when the Duke of Zhongfu was stationed at Bozhou, he invited Chan Master Yong of the Huayan Monastery in Yingzhou to visit him.

There, he was able to hear the teachings on the mind-dharma. Later, upon his retirement and residence in Luoyang, he composed a verse to express his aspirations and sent it to Chan Master Yuanzhao of Gusu, the master from whom Yong had received the Dharma, saying:
"I personally saw Master Yong and attained deep realization; Through successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of my teacher."
"To the southeast, one might idly speak of the distance between mountains and rivers, yet here my eyes face both the Lingguang and Miaoyin [Pagodas].

Furthermore, there was a letter which stated: 'I, Bi, have devoted myself to the ancestral Way for many days. I have always regretted not encountering a person of clear vision to enlighten my ignorance and coarseness.

Although I have long heard of your eminent virtue, I had no means to pay you my respects. Yesterday, by good fortune, I was appointed as Governor of Boshè, whose borders adjoin those of Yíngzhōu. Consequently...'"
Zhang Bubing of Jingshan, a resident of the village, invited Master Yongyong to visit him.

They stayed together for nearly a month, during which time, through the power of his compassion and skillful means, the Master enabled me to attain moments of awakening. However, as the summer retreat was approaching, I hastily returned to Ying in the fourth month.
Regarding the refinement and purification of my practice, I have made little progress; old ailments persist, and my dullness makes it difficult to enter the Way.
What the ancient Master Guling spoke of—that one would unexpectedly encounter the ultimate matter upon reaching old age—is seen in Bi today.
What a great fortune! What a great fortune! Although Bi received the Dharma from Master Yong, its ultimate source flows from you, Old Monk;
the lineage is most direct. I must certainly uphold it as well, and thus I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant me your guidance. Far-reaching grace!
To guide and lead others—bringing those who have not yet reached the goal to that very attainment—is precisely what was done by Pang Yun under Nanyue and Pei Xiu under Baizhang.
How could they differ? Your Excellency’s nobility reached the pinnacle of ministerial rank, yet you suddenly awakened to this Way; you may truly be called a man of immeasurable capacity.

Furthermore, you were able to expound upon the meaning of the Dharma for Yuanzhao and recount the history of our lineage. By citing the Elder Guling, who only managed to hear the ultimate teaching as he approached old age, [you demonstrate the rarity of such an opportunity].
Thus, he speaks of his own affairs; how could he be deceiving others?
The Shu monk Zuxiu, styled Zizhi, was early on renowned for his literary talent among the scholar-officials.

Admiring the style of Sengming of Mount Song, he composed the "External Biography of Lord Wenyong of the Ouyang Family. Su Yangzhi (Su Xiang) wrote a preface to head the work. A brief [account follows].
He said: "The gentleman observes that the Buddha’s teachings were not attested during the eras of Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang.

Yet, after Confucius and Mencius, successive generations of former scholars, though they held power in the state, did not prohibit them in the slightest; they likewise allowed them to flow unchecked throughout the realm.
There have been those throughout antiquity who maintained this argument. However, Master Dushou [Dunlun] considered that Danzhu, the son of Yao, was insufficient [to serve as a precedent]."
Having entrusted the administration, Yao abdicated in favor of Shun; Shun, likewise concerned for Shangjun, abdicated in favor of Yu.

It was with the "revolution" of Tang and Wu that this teaching first began. Had Confucius been acting in such a manner, how would it have differed from this? From Yao down to King Wu, the Buddha had not yet appeared; there was a reason for this.
Once Cheng and Kang had passed away, the Buddha then manifested his traces; however, he had not yet reached the Central Kingdom.
[The Master] Hua waited for the Sage to be born in Lu so that he might synthesize the great achievement of the teachings of the ancient emperors. How dire it was!
The Sage encountered hardship in Lu, Wei, Chen, and Song; he wished to dwell among the nine tribes of the Yi and rode upon a raft to float across the sea.

At that time, had the teachings from tens of thousands of li abroad been applied to the Middle Kingdom, who—among the Son of Heaven or the feudal lords—would have listened to them? As for the Buddha’s...
The Dharma is not transmitted lightly; it is only when one is moved by the manifestation of the True Doctrine that one seeks it from afar. I fear it may not respond swiftly otherwise.

These were all letters from Master Xiu to the capital, wherein his arguments that startle the ancients and shake the present overflowed for tens of thousands of words, yet they have not been transmitted to the world.
Furthermore, Xiu once praised a portrait of Dongpo, saying: "Among the Sima, Yang, and Wang of the Han, and the Taibai of the Tang..."
Zi’ang. These five gentlemen were all born in Shu Commandery, yet none possessed the brilliant luster of our Master.
As for poetry that rivals his, there is perhaps only Subei; as for prose that vies with him, there is perhaps only Zichang.
His fu compositions surpass those of Qu Yuan and Jia Yi, and his calligraphy is more robust than that of Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi. These are the Master’s peerless skills.
Indeed, [the current state] is like the chaff and straw of the Ultimate Way. Your Way, Master, is that of Houji and Yi Yin; it is capable of leading one's sovereign to the heights of Yao and Tang.
While contemporary discourse would subject you to the executioner’s axe and sword, you, Master, remain particularly attuned to the principles of the ancient statutes.

To those migrating beyond the seas, it is like returning to one’s native village. Among those who truly believe in the "Five Eminences" of Shu Commandery, none are able to peer behind the walls of the Master.
As for Xiu’s discourses and literary style, they do not end here alone; one may know the flavor of the entire cauldron by tasting a single morsel.
At the beginning of the Jingkang era, while Xiu was still staying in the capital, he composed the *Huayang Gong Ji* (Record of the Huayang Palace), which is exceedingly detailed and comprehensive.
The *Dongdu Shilüe* (Brief History of the Eastern Capital) contains a biographical eulogy for Zhu Min.
Indeed, for those who oversee his service, the so-called Mount Shou and Mount Gen are already perfectly clear; what need is there to cast one's gaze upon them?
Chancellor Zhang De-yuan, while serving as Governor of Fudang, invited Master Xiu to reside at Guangyan Hermitage in Changle. Later, he retired to Shushan, where he dwelt in tranquil seclusion. One—
In a single word he spoke, he never forgot to protect the lineage and defend the teachings. Since his merit did not equal his wisdom, he was held in high esteem by contemporary discourse.
Zen Master Ji of Dongshan in Xingan was a native of Min; he was the preceptor under whom Master Guang of Fozhao received his ordination. His mastery of the Way was profound.
Fengmao was eloquent and possessed a free-flowing, unencumbered manner of speech; eminent scholars delighted in associating with him.

There was a man named Li Chaoqing, who was the maternal uncle of the Layman Xianglin. Once, while accompanying Xianglin to visit Fengmao to discuss the Way, Li asked, "When the 'house-thief' troubles one, what then?
Fengmao replied, "Who is the house-thief? Li raised his fist. Fengmao said, "The thief's own body has already been revealed."
Li said, "Master, do not deceive people. Ji said, "The evidence is right here before you. Li stared in astonishment, unable to respond. Ji spontaneously uttered a verse:
"The house-thief vexes the person—how can one deal with him? Even the thousand sages turn their faculties back only for his sake."

Pervading the world and pervading space, it leaves no trace; without dependence and without abiding, it is beyond all nets and snares. Thief! Thief! Neither fierce generals nor heroic soldiers can capture him.
He would have murdered the old Chan masters of the world and made the ancient Maitreya in the bustling marketplace fall over with laughter.
Stop! Stop! There is no need to seek the mind outwardly. In a single glance back, the thief’s own body is revealed; caught together with his loot, he has no peer in the world.

Peerless in this world, truly worthy of veneration. From now on, I shall no longer boast of my skills; when we rely upon one another in peace and joy, the myriad phenomena of the universe will all clap their hands in unison.
Ji You once expressed the essence of Deshan and Linji’s “staff and shout” through two verses, saying:
"The moment one enters the gate, there is a blow; though one may be thrown into sevenfold confusion, the entire earth and heavens are simultaneously seen through."
Upon entering, he let out a shout. The yakṣas, rākṣasas, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all simultaneously broke into a violent rage.
Ji was the successor of Master Lin of Daochang Mountain. Later, while presiding over the assembly at Kaiyuan Temple in Southern Min, during the midday meal in the Cloud Hall, he spoke this verse:
"An old bhikṣu of eighty-four years; Of all the myriad arrangements, none are better than ceasing. This morning, all is vast and open."

Forgetting all conditions, he departed. He remained indifferent to the saying that "the bridge flows, but the water does not flow," and then passed away peacefully. Such was the extraordinary nature of his demeanor when facing this great transformation.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Huangyou era, Emperor Renzong dispatched an imperial messenger to deliver a personal inquiry.
At Jingyin Dajue Chan Master Huailian, [Wuzhuo] said, "As soon as you raise your whisk, no one will be able to withstand you. Just then, Huailian was serving morning congee to the assembly;

he immediately rose to express his gratitude and invited the imperial messenger to join them for the meal. After the congee was finished, Wuzhuo presented a verse in return, saying: [Verse omitted per instructions]

"Having joints, yet not made of bamboo; three stars encircle the lunar palace. One person dwells beneath the sun; he is not the same as the common crowd. Thereupon, the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased.
Shortly thereafter, he further bestowed a verse, saying: "The most excellent monk in seated meditation; having forgotten artifice, thoughts do not arise.
With no-mind, the flames have already been extinguished; I treasure you, past, present, and future. Liai responded in harmony and presented it, saying: "The most excellent..."
For a monk practicing seated meditation, there is neither thought nor arising; it is like the bright moon appearing in a clear pool. Who can speak of "ancient" and "present"?
At that time, Master Long of Huayan once remarked that Lia’s verse on “The Mind Itself is Buddha” was merely like driving a wedge into empty space.
However, Master Lia’s response to the Imperial inquiry was appropriate to the occasion. That Master Long spoke thus—each had their own underlying intent.
Whenever Chan Master Huanglong Nan saw a student arrive, he would invariably ask about their "birth-conditions," the "Buddha’s hand," and the "donkey’s feet.
Consequently, the monastic community designated these as the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan). He also composed three verses himself to clarify their underlying meaning;

however, the world has transmitted only those concerning the Buddha’s hand and the donkey’s feet, while omitting the one on birth-conditions. Master Min of Lushan Yuan Tong was a Dharma-grandson of Huanglong.
At the place of the senior seat-holder Guangbian on Mount Nanyue, he saw three verses written in Nanyue’s own hand, which said: "My hand and the Buddha's hand are raised together;
May the Chan practitioner directly realize this. Without moving a blade of grass, the Way emerges; Right where one stands, one transcends Buddhas and patriarchs."

My feet and the donkey’s feet walk side by side; at every step, I tread upon the Unborn. When you realize that the clouds have gathered and the sun has rolled up, only then will you know this Way extends in all directions.
Those with karmic conditions for birth recognize the words of others, yet how could the water jelly ever separate from the shrimp?
Seeing only the sun rising in the east, who would go on to drink Zhaozhou’s tea? If one relies on the *Línjiānlù* (Record of the Forest) regarding the Buddha...
In the collated edition of the *Verses on the Hands, Donkey, Feet, and Neck*, there are eleven characters that differ; could this not be due to successive revisions?

For instance, when Master Nan presented his verse on the "Examining the Old Woman" story to Ciming, he still distinguished between skill and clumsiness based on whether certain characters were present or absent.
Judging from this, how could there not be distinctions of superiority and inferiority?
In Chongling there is a stream called Lan. This was where Zhou Gong Maoshu’s ancestors once resided;
having found joy in the secluded beauty of Mount Lu, he built a dwelling there and named the brook Lan, thereby acknowledging that one should not forget one's roots.
At that time, the Chan Master Foyin Yuanwu resided above Luan Creek, and they studied the Way together as friends beyond the secular world. It was for this reason that [the name] was bestowed.

Foyin served as the head of the Qing Song Society, emulating the precedent of the White Lotus Society. During the Jiayou era, the Master was serving as an Acting Governor in Gan County when he was slandered by someone to the local Inspector.
The Inspector confronted him with great severity, yet the Master remained transcendent and unperturbed.
Hearing of this, Foyin composed the "Lushan Yiwen" (A Memorial to Mount Lu) and sent it to him, saying: "The winds and waves of the official path are all cause for alarm; only your mind..."
The earth is level and vast. Before speaking of worldly gain, his brows knit; as soon as he gazes upon the clouds and mountains, his eyes grow clear.
The lake residence is near, with willow colors dividing the embankments; the field hermitage newly occupies the sound of the stone brook.

Green pines have already been pledged for a Zen community; do not let white hairs sprout by the time you return. While the Master had not yet returned, [the author] again urged him, saying: "I often think of the intimacy at Lake Mouth."
It is different. Furthermore, I recall our extensive travels at Mount Kuang-lu; the mountains and rivers of both places have frequently appeared before my eyes.
Ten years of wind and moon have passed with quiet serenity through autumn. Who can provide the elixirs of the immortals? Yet the world of the Buddha-land may naturally find rest.

Moreover, there is the appointment for the Lotus Society at Tiantai Lake; when shall we join hands to converse upon the mountain peaks? Although you, sir, pursue the study of exhausting all principles, you nonetheless recommend the Buddha.
Yin served as the head of the community. Since our paths are different, how could we possibly consult with one another?

To the south of the mountain is the Hot Spring of Mount Lu; it is a small monastery. During the Xining era, Chan Gong resided there as the abbot, and the monastic community was likewise harmonious and solemn.
He once related that Nanquan, along with Guizong and Magu, went to pay their respects to the National Teacher. On the way, at a certain spot on the ground...
He drew a single circle and said, "If you can speak, then you may go. Zong immediately sat within the circle; Gu bowed like a woman.
Quan said, "In that case, you shall not go. Zong asked, "What kind of mental activity is this? Quan then called him back. Chan then composed a verse, saying:
"A single palm does not ring out recklessly; The numinous light exists in each and every one. As soon as a single Buddhist temple is established,"
"Everyone, lend a hand! Master Dahui is once again presiding over Jingshan. He therefore exhorted his disciples to take up the alms bowl, and he also cited this [verse] on occasion.
Chan Gong was a successor of Zhenjing.
Yangshan Xiaoshijia resided at Guanyin Monastery in Yuzhang. The monk Qi Ji served as the general supervisor of administrative affairs.

He composed a preface for the morning gruel, which stated: "Gruel is called a 'good medicine,' praised by the Buddha. Its meaning surpasses the three kinds of giving, and its merit is marked by ten benefits.

We further pray that the wise and noble may each fulfill their aspirational hearts; having prepared this at the break of dawn, may it forever support pure karma. This was formerly engraved upon stone, and since it has already passed...

During the military fires of the Jianyan era, nothing remained of it. The *Zhifang cheng* (Voyage through the Provinces) of Yuzhang merely states that the Buddhist poet Qiji composed these verses for the morning gruel;

while the calligraphy he inscribed is worth viewing, its literary content was not recorded. Today, in the Zen monasteries, only the first four lines of the morning gruel chant are recited, and it is not even known who composed them.
Qiji’s secular surname was Hu; he was a native of Yiyang in Tan province. From his youth, he renounced [the world].
In secular life, he followed Master Daoyou at Daguai; thus, he was a fellow disciple of Master Huizhi. Later, he resided at Jingu on Mount Xishan and passed away there.
His stupa still exists at Longpan, which was his study hall. During the Yuanyou era, Ma Duyun Chun composed a short poem inscribed on the wall of the monastery, which says:
"Zhidun’s carefree wandering did not meet mine; I casually dismounted my horse to rest."
The Lotus Palace. [He] wished to inquire about the secluded life of Qi Ji, but the seventy-year-old mountain monk’s ears were deaf.
Chan Master Cong Cizhao resided at Shimen in Xiangzhou; he requested that Imperial Commissioner Cha compose a record for the Sangha Hall, stating:
"As for Qianming Temple, it is one hundred *li* from the prefectural seat. It was anciently called Shimen, but its name was changed by imperial decree. It is situated on a high mountain..."

Leng Valley is a place where tigers and leopards lie in wait; its paths are rugged and stony, and human habitation is utterly remote. None who do not set their will upon the Way can find a place to settle their minds here.
Among those who travel for official service, bound as they are by profit and fame, few are able to ascend these heights even though they behold their magnificent seclusion.

During my tenure as the Prefectural Governor of Daozhou, I learned that there was a student of the Dharma named Fashourong, whose courtesy name was Shorong, from the third year of the Renshou era. From Yongxi—
He arrived there in search of [the Dharma] in his later years. Later, as the hall for seated meditation had become low, cramped, and dilapidated, he resolved to rebuild it.
Fortifying his resolve, he traveled through the villages to seek alms over many years. He summoned skilled craftsmen and purchased fine timber;
by the third year of the Jingde era, the work was finally completed. It consisted of five bays and eleven structural frames. In the spring, his disciple Huiguo took up his staff and...
Upon arriving at the capital, he requested that I provide an inscription for it, intending to have it carved upon stone. I then wrote this:

"Since the Buddha-dharma spread widely and Bodhidharma came from the West, those endowed with the faculty of faith have sought to realize the original source. Dwelling like stars in the vast wilderness, they sheltered themselves among grasses and trees;
their clothing did not ward off the cold, and their food did not fill the belly. Yet, as the True Dharma gradually became diluted and human practice grew lax, Master Baizhang..."
They constructed halls and buildings to provide shelter for the elderly and the infirm. Lately, Zen monasteries have vied with one another to build grand and magnificent structures.
Young beginners lie at ease within them, utterly unaware that those who labor to raise funds exhaust their bodies and bones, while those who donate wealth seek merit and repent their sins.

To one who understands cause and effect, such a place is like lying upon an iron bed or facing a mortal enemy; were it not for the fact that they must diligently increase their practice day and night, [they would surely fall into ruin].

One nurtures the holy embryo. Next, as for those who draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they resolve to seek liberation; their physical forms may be temporarily sustained, and they are protected by dragons and deities.

Yet, if their minds are turbid and entangled by the afflictions (kleśa), though their bodies remain warm and comfortable, they fail to examine ignorance (avidyā) and do not realize that their lifespan is diminishing.
Merely memorizing words and phrases, they claim to have reached the ultimate goal. When their vigor is exhausted and they pass away, they fall into those evil realms. O noble man!

How fiercely determined he was to attain an unshakable mind! Master Rong was born in Guo County of Fengxiang. He left the household life at Jingju Chan Monastery on Baiyun Mountain in Hu County, Yongzhou.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, he recorded this according to what has been transmitted by the world;
it begins from the time the Buddha-dharma was widely disseminated and concludes with his attainment of an unshakable mind.
Therefore, Grand Historian Huang replied in a letter to Zhitánxiù: "Master Chá was a renowned scholar of the previous dynasty who studied under the gates of Yang Wénɡōng and Wáng Wénhuìɡōng;
he was one who possessed true vitality in his practice of Chan and the Way. However, this record of the monk’s hall likely still lacks its beginning and end.
Master Chá participated early on in the assembly of National Teacher Lángxié Jué, where he personally attended to the tasks of fetching water and chopping wood."
Because Langya showed him the commentary on the Third Patriarch’s *Xinxin Ming*, he wrote one phrase in large characters above and another in small characters below.
After several phrases, he suddenly attained enlightenment to the essential meaning. Jue then told him:
"This old monk has been merely painting empty space; you must spit it all out before you can succeed. Master Miaoxi once remarked that during the Daguan era...
I heard from an elder in Taiping Prefecture that it was indeed so.
Chan Master Caigen, whose secular name was Cai, first received his monastic precepts at his home monastery and followed the local customs of the time.
Consequently, he went to Chengdu to procure ritual implements. There, he encountered an old man who said to him, "You yourself are already a vessel of the Dharma; why seek elsewhere? Cai—

Suddenly, he had a powerful realization. He immediately went to the Dharma seat at Xichan Monastery. There he heard the Abbot, Chan Master Haiyin Long, say: "In my life, when sleeping I have never fallen behind others; when rising, I have never fallen behind others. He then secretly came to admire these words. Later, seeing an elderly master who had attained the Way reading a sutra, he reached the passage: "At a single hair-tip, a lion appears; at ten billion hair-tips, they all appear simultaneously. As soon as he saw this, he pointed to it and asked: [The master replied: "This is the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body. He then said: "If that is so, then why does the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* say, 'The Buddha-body is like empty space, pervading the ten directions'? The master was speechless. He then went to see Chan Master Wuxue Zuyuan, who asked him: "Where have you come from? He replied: "From the place where there is no coming. The master said: "If there is no coming, how can you have come here? He replied: "Though there is no coming, I have already arrived. The master said: "If you have already arrived, where are you now? He replied: "I am not in the place where there is no coming. The master said: "If you are not in the place where there is no coming, then where are you? He replied: "I am in the place where there is no non-coming. The master said: "If you are in the place where there is no non-coming, then what is the place where there is no non-coming? He replied: "It is precisely because there is no non-coming that it is called the place where there is no non-coming. The master said: "If there is no non-coming, how can there be a place where there is no non-coming? He replied: "Because there is no non-coming, there is a place where there is no non-coming. The master said: "If there is no non-coming, how can there be a place where there is no non-coming? If there is a place where there is no non-coming, then there must be a non-coming. He replied: "If there were a non-coming, then there would indeed be a place where there is no non-coming. But since there is no non-coming, how could there be a place where there is no non-coming? The master said: "If there is no non-coming, then how can you say there is a place where there is no non-coming? He replied: "If there were a non-coming, then there would be a place where there is no non-coming. But since there is no non-coming, how could there be a place where there is no non-coming? The master said: "If there is no non-coming, then how can you say there is a place where there is no non-coming? "Is this permissible? When Lián heard this, he reviled him for violating the rites of respect and obedience, severely rebuking and expelling him. At that time, the laborers were pruning the cypress trees in the courtyard.
Facing the southern entrance, he composed the "Verses on Washing the Cypress" (*Xǐbǎi jì*) to express his intent, saying:

Two cold cypresses planted before the steps, Their verdant leaves and numinous roots grow ever firmer. Having naturally inherited a noble character for ten thousand years, Do not treat them with indifference amidst frost and snow.
They burned each other with mutual resentment. Lián was struck by this as strange. When he reached the age of nineteen, he registered in the monastic rolls (*saṃgha-nikāya*).
Thereupon, he and a fellow monk from the same monastery, Hǎipíng, performed the *Liángwǔ Chàn* (the Repentance Rite of Emperor Wǔ) as patrons. Suddenly, overcome with emotion, he said to Píng:

"If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the ancestors of our school, yet we cannot fully know their origins; and even when reading the liturgical texts of the repentance rite, we still err in the characters and phrases—how much more so regarding the profound mysteries!"
Is this not meaningful? Now that you have taken a mere physical likeness as your heir, do you not feel a sense of shame? Thereafter, he visited Master Tán of Kāiyuán Temple in the commandery.
While they were appreciating the moon, Tán asked his disciples to compose verses to express their aspirations. Nán immediately responded:
"On the fifteenth night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the bright moon shines upon the azure stream; it is not only above the Yīn River, but its light fills all four hundred prefectures. Tán...

He was delighted, remarking that [the Master’s] capacity was not easily measured. Soon after, he traveled to the region of Jiangxi, first visiting the quarters of Master Xian of Longqing in Luling, and subsequently calling upon Master Wei of Yangshan;
both held him in high esteem. In the *Jiwei* year of the Yuanfeng era (1079), he arrived at Daolin in Changsha to pay his respects to Chan Master You.
Under You’s instruction, his doubts were suddenly resolved. After You retired from his administrative duties at the monastery, [he followed him].

He attended Mount Lu. By the year Wuyin of the Yuanyou era, Foyou was residing at Luohan Monastery. Nanfuchang established a monastic community there that stood preeminent throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.

Consequently, Foyou retired, and Nan succeeded him on the seat; at that time, he was thirty-nine years old. In managing affairs and caring for the assembly, his character and regulations were strict and orderly.
His reputation for the Way spread in all directions. Having spent seventy years [in the monastic life], he suddenly ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:

Today, the Arhat rode backward upon an iron horse, ascending Mount Sumeru in reverse and trampling through the void without leaving a single trace, before returning to his quarters and passing away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
This was indeed in the first year of the Shaoxing era, the Jiaxu year. His disciple Xingchu collected these events and commissioned the Sichuan monk Yunping to record them in sequence;
it may be said that this account is exhaustive. The *Xu sengbao zhuan* (Continued Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) records it as "Nan."
As for the beginning, since its details cannot be fully ascertained, is this not like "feeling the elephant"?
Chan Master Zong of Meishan Yuchiu in Chizhou was staying overnight in the mountains while Hong Qingshan, a lay practitioner of Liantang, was on official duty in Jiangdong.
They engaged in a night conversation, during which Hong asked: "In which sutra is the feeding of monks mentioned? His...
"What is the essential meaning? Zong said, "The *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* states: 'Feeding a hundred evil people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person;
even feeding a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not as good as feeding one who dwells nowhere, acts nowhere, and realizes nothing.
This state of non-cultivation and non-realization is precisely right mindfulness and solitary liberation. To be able to feed such a person is to transcend all merit."
"O Buddhas! However, many predecessors have known this principle. Hong asked, "Who were they? Zong replied, "To speak of recent examples:
when Qin Shaoyou was in his place of exile in Tengzhou, he composed his own funeral elegy, containing the line, 'Who will provide the meal for the yellow-robed monks?
When Dongpo heard of Qin's plan, he sent five taels of silver by letter, entrusting Fan Yuanzhang to [arrange it]."
When Qin provided a meal for the monks, and Dongpo was returning from the north and arrived at Pilin, he did not rise due to illness.

A student of the Imperial Academy collected money in Dongjing Huilin Temple to provide a meal for the monks; this was recorded at the beginning of the epitaph for Dongpo composed by Su Huangmen. Hong said:
"Is there scriptural authority for the practice of giving monetary gifts? Zong replied, "Have you not seen the 'Luming' (The Call of the Deer) in the Xiao Ya (Minor Odes) of the Mao Shi?

It describes the entertaining of ministers and honored guests; having provided them with food and drink, one further fills their purses and baskets with silks and fabrics to convey one's profound sincerity.
This is because mere food and drink are insufficient to fully express reverence, and thus additional gifts are bestowed to manifest earnest devotion. Thereupon, he recited the passage by Ding.

The Memorial for the Ordination of Monks by Duke Jin states: "The Buddha bestowed universal wisdom, and the Way nurtures all living beings. Whenever one seeks to rescue those in peril and distress, one must first manifest auspicious responses.
I, a layman, have sought official emolument and have been granted the heavy authority of the Grand Chancellor;

at the Crimson Steps, I have proclaimed imperial grace, having been favored with the abundant bounty of the late Sovereign. Like Zhongshan, I have mended the dragon robes, exhausting my skillful mind; like Fu Yue, I [harmonized the cauldron]..."
Regarding the soup: it was difficult to satisfy the diverse palates of the multitude. While he was resting in peaceful sleep, he suddenly dreamed of a pure countenance.

The wondrous instruction was clear and resonant, causing his defiled mind to awaken early; yet the true form remained faint and obscured, leaving him to lament that his ordinary eyes could not perceive it.

Because his wisdom had not encompassed all aspects and his actions failed to avoid danger, when calamity arrived it was unfathomable, resulting in an extraordinary disaster. He was banished to the Western Capital, where he was moved by the Sage.

Out of grace, you have shown me clemency and banished me to the southern frontiers. While I, Zhongxian, would have preferred to die with a willing heart, my guilt was truly self-inflicted; this calamity was not wrought by another.
Now that my family is scattered across distant lands, how can I hope to return ten thousand *li* away? Having already become a minister who has betrayed the state, I am filled with remorse.

Having forever severed the arts of governing the state, he traveled through the lands of Xiang. Finding refuge on a sacred mountain, while still possessing a body subject to affliction, he suddenly encountered a community of those who dwell in cool serenity.
Only then did he realize that wealth and status cannot be maintained from beginning to end; even the glory of feasting at the imperial cauldron is no exception.

How could this compare to the excellence of a bowl of soup? I have specifically manifested my taking refuge and reverently aroused sincere devotion to piously bestow white gold for the purpose of preparing pure offerings.
I shall feed the high-virtue bhikṣus to repay the profound compassion of Làn Zàn. I hope that he may preserve this practice and be spared from any ailment.

I prostrate myself and pray that Heaven will turn its southern favor and grant its grace from above, sparing him from being placed among the border tribes, so that his days may be as bright as the sun.

While in the realm of hungry ghosts, he was granted a return to the Central Kingdom; thus, the Yellow Springs once again felt the grace of Heaven. With utmost sincerity, he reverently exhausted his devotion, forever relying upon the power of the Dharma.
Hong remarked: "Previously, when reading the *Biographies of Illustrious Ministers*, I saw only the couplet concerning 'replenishing Zhongsan’s robes' and 'harmonizing Fu Yue’s broth.
Now I have heard it in its entirety; such was the nature of his refined prayers."
When Chan Master Huihong Shixin was with the Sichuan monk Quan Fayong, as they were entering the room for instruction, Shixin said, "I hear you are skilled at composing poetry;
try reciting a verse. Quan replied, "Please, Master, provide a topic. Shixin held up his whisk.
Quan said, "A single line attained while seated; a fragment of mind comes from beyond the heavens. Shixin remarked, "Chuan Lajue has lost the rhyme."
Yuanquan said, "The corrupt examiners are as numerous as hemp and millet. With that, he shook out his sleeves and departed. Shortly thereafter, Sishin spoke these words:
"Elder Huanglong, you have touched upon affliction; if one were to discuss the ground of the mind, the red sun shines brightly.

There is a version where "touched upon affliction" (*chuzhe fan’nao*) is changed to "headless and brainless" (*wutou wunao*). Upon hearing this, Sishin became enraged and reviled him. Yuanquan said, "This is precisely..."
He said, "This brings glory to my teacher. Sishin said, "A monk from Chuanshou, why do you come here with such a clumsy leg?
Quan said, "The Patriarch’s verse says: 'The true nature is hidden in the heart-ground; it has neither head nor tail. Is that not also a clumsy leg?
Sishin could not help but smile. Sishin once praised the Sixth Patriarch, saying: "The Sixth Patriarch was no great man of his time; he asked another to write on the wall for him..."

Tuhu: Although it is clearly stated in the verse that "there is no thing," he nevertheless accepted a single bowl from another house. At that time, there were many who composed verses in response to its rhyme.

Sīxīn (Sīxìn) again used the original rhyme to offer a reply to Quán, saying: "A single quatrain, brilliant and refined, surpasses a man of worth; His every word and breath is not like a coarse barbarian.
One must know that attaining the meaning is like flowing water— It brings a laugh that puts even Huángméi to shame."
They contended over the alms bowl. Quan then took his leave with a verse that contained the line: "The Patriarch’s intent came from the West; I do not know it.

Sisi immediately picked up this line and sent it back to him, saying: "The Patriarch’s intent came from the West; I do not know it. When you know it, you have not yet entered the realm beyond differentiation (liwei).
Only when you have thoroughly realized the principle of non-differentiation Will you believe in the source of mind and return to it alone."
Chan Master Xuedou Chi succeeded Master Xiangtian Qing. He was the grandson of Donglin Zhaojue. In his daily life, his verses and hymns were composed spontaneously as they emerged from his mouth.
Regarding his composition on a paper curtain, he wrote: "Neither violating the rules of silk nor involving mechanical artifice, Gently rubbed upon frost-white mulberry paper, it is pure and fitting.
The autumn moon fills half the hall, making night indistinguishable; A single bed of cold clouds has not yet dispersed. Sleeping away..."

Vast and untrammeled, one forgets the primordial chaos (*chun-hun*). Sitting thus in empty clarity, one is called "Non-Action" (*wu-wei*). Continuous and subtle, not allowing even a speck of dust to enter—let the wind blow from all eight directions as it pleases.
Furthermore, regarding the artificial mountain: A few fist-sized stones are piled high and steep; the pond water is deep and still, with not a ripple of an inch.
Once you recognize the infinite meaning of mountains and rivers, there is no need for much more than this present serenity. Again, *Xian*.
Jū said: "In recent years, my heart has had no desire for worldly affairs; my plan to dwell alone on a solitary peak is already set.
When there is a moment of joy, what can one do? I let out two or three long whistles as I circle the pines. Master Dàhuì formerly resided at Jìngshān.
His Dharma assembly was so magnificent that the various mountain monasteries never dared to even approach his gate. Yet [Jū] alone went to pay his respects. Dàhuì received him with the highest honor.
During a lecture in the hall, while the members of the Dharma family were together viewing a painting of Linji, Dahui Zhi held the original and wished to transmit it.
Dahui instructed that the image be altered to show him with his sleeves rolled up and his fist clenched in the *zhuan* (the "pointing" gesture). Zhi then composed this eulogy for it:
"His face resembles a heap of wet ashes; His shout is like the wrathful thunder of a drought-stricken sky. Though he is coarse and rugged, He does not shrink from the truth."
"Kua kua! Tui! What is this? If you do not grasp this principle, you will surely become a ringleader."
Subsequently, there were those in various regions who painted portraits of his crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), imitating him by making him appear with bared elbows and clenched fists;

they could not avoid being ridiculed by those with discernment. Huidi was particularly skilled at wit and humor, speaking with sharp and quick repartee. There was a man named Fan, a prominent figure among those who preyed upon scholars;
he entered the temple and feasted insatiably. One day, after finishing his meal, Fan walked about rubbing his belly. Huidi asked him about it.
"Do you have an ailment in your stomach? Fan replied immediately, "I am honored to serve as a practitioner of the Daoist tradition’s methods for nurturing life. As it is said:
'After eating, walk a hundred paces and quickly rub your belly with your hands. He then responded to him, saying: 'If you wish to learn the art of longevity...'"
"Your 'unchanging' is my 'eternal abiding. " Because of this, Fan withdrew in shame and never returned again.
Zen Master Longya, whose name was Congmi and courtesy name Shishu, was highly prized by the world for his calligraphy in the cursive script (*cǎoshèng*).
Zhang Huaisu of Shu styled himself the "Luo-puo Wild Man" and traveled among the high officials using illusory arts. In the fourth year of the Chongning era, Huaisu—

Su was plotting a rebellion when his scheme failed; he was subjected to the slow slicing punishment and executed by beheading. Upon searching his satchel, a document written in secret cursive script (*mìcǎoshū*) was found.

Master Hong Juefan appended a colophon to it, whereby the two masters were implicated and subsequently punished. Later, Mi returned to Min, whereupon he composed a verse that says: "On Changting there is an old *dhūta*;
With sudden realization, he considers how much evil karma he has amassed. Fearing that old age will add white hairs to his head,"

Startled, he gallops through the surging waves of the Yellow River; he flees for cover to the ends of the earth and the corners of the sea. He passes the sword-trees and knife-mountains in the blink of an eye.
Today, returning south, he still lives. Let others laugh that he does not resemble a Zen monk.

He once composed a verse on the four elements, which says: "Earth, wind, fire, and water originally have no root; now, borrowing from their source, they serve as your honored self. When the six functions cease, the person..."
"Not seen. In a state of empty mechanism, where do I exist? Cease seeking the patriarchs in dryness or dampness;
do not recognize 'sons and grandsons' in what is firm or shifting. Remembering the words of Master Zeng, they are all truly appropriate—altogether like a broken sand pot.
In the evening of that year, while residing at Dongchan Temple in Fuzhou, [Mimi] invited Zheng Bianxiu Shangming for a meal. He personally brewed tea and said: "I..."
"A great matter has arrived; I ask you, sir, to bear witness. He then asked, "Have you ever received my cursive calligraphy of the *Qianziwen*?
Zheng replied, "I have not yet had the honor of receiving such a gift. The Master then took up his brush and wrote the *Qianziwen* in cursive script;
it was far superior to his usual work. He then requested paper and wrote a verse: "Having exhausted seventy autumns among the world, All myriad conditions now cease at once. The void..."
He shattered all mundane affairs; a whole ox, its body revealed on the open ground, was startled awake. He cast down his brush and passed away.
Upon cremation, wherever the smoke reached, there were śarīras of five colors.
Chan Master Huiyao Ying of Hengzhou was the son of the Li family from Hukou on the Yangtze River. Initially, he received the transmission of the Dharma under Zhenjing;
he subsequently went to Yunju, where Foyin appointed him as the head of the assembly. One day, Foyin clenched his fist and asked, "Head Seat, what do you make of this?
Ying replied, "In the future, I shall not dare forget the Master. Foyin privately considered this a source of joy.
A verse was sent to him, saying: "Who can recognize the hero of Jizhou? His beak is forged from the iron of Silla. He will never follow the flocks of crows and magpies;
Calling out two or three times, he gazes at the clouds in leisure. This was intended to praise his sharp wit and eloquence.

Consequently, the monastic community called him "Iron-Beak Hero" (Ying Tie-zui). In the autumn of the first year of the Shaosheng era, he received the *kaishan* (abbatial) seal at Yunju under Master Tan.
Fukumei became the successor to Zhenjing. From then on, every winter and summer, he invariably sent inquiries after his well-being and presented robes and necessities.
He forbade the use of servants as messengers and instead sent letters at the beginning of each month. Yet Zhenjing had nothing whatsoever to send in return;

he did so only when approaching his passing, entrusting him with his yellow *kāṣāya*. Upon receiving the news of the funeral and inheriting the robe, Ying collapsed to the ground wailing in grief. Dahui—
The Master spoke of him in this way, further stating that among those devoted to the Dharma and its meaning under his guidance, none had surpassed the brilliant and incisive Iron Beak (Tie-zui).
During the Xining era, there was a monk named Qingshun, whose style name was Yiran; he resided in a magnificent location on the mountains surrounding West Lake and frequented Lingyin Temple.
Yin of India expressed his leisurely pleasures in verse, saying: "Wandering freely, I chant beneath the emerald peaks; Not a single dharma remains for contemplation.
If someone asks about my intent in leaving the mountains, I carry a tattered robe upon the tip of my staff of mugwort.
He also said: "In every matter I am incapable, unable to advance even one step; Joyfully returning to India, I shall pass the remaining years. When hungry, I eat; when weary,"
He lay down with no other concerns; let us cease speaking of how there is another heaven within the flask.
Prime Minister Shi Lin Ye Shaoyun remarked that Shun was pure, frugal, upright, and serene; he did not arbitrarily associate with others and did not enter cities except for grave reasons.
When officials and gentlemen went to visit him, some would occasionally present him with rice, yet what he accepted never exceeded several *dou*, which he stored in a jar.
Place it on a small table and consume two or three portions daily. Although it is a vegetable dish, it is not always available.

When东坡 (Dongpo) was in Lingnan, he once sent someone to West Lake with these words: "The Venerable Chuiyun Shun was a poetic companion with whom I exchanged verses during my tenure as Regional Inspector.
He was pure and upright yet extremely poor; his food barely sufficed for him, falling short at times."
Yet he never once showed a look of anxiety. "I am old now; I do not know if I shall still remain robust. Alas!

Today, our contemporaries regard pure poverty as a shame and consider great accumulation of wealth a source of honor. When their lives suddenly come to an end, it is rare that they do not leave their followers in bonds and fetters.
Had they but admired the spirit of Shun even slightly, how could they have left behind such a foul legacy?
When Academician Wang Yanzhang was governing Xiuxi, he lamented that he had heard of the Way too late in life.

Whenever he had a day of leave from his duties, he would invariably meet with the elders of the various mountains to engage in spiritual discourse. He then thought of Xixi Cishou, Daochang Puming, and Heshan Fudeng.
While sitting in his study, he noticed there was an image of the Monk with the Cloth Bag on the wall; it was a famous painting. Thereupon, the Master...
Pointing [at the painting], he asked the various masters of the mountains, "How would you rate this?

Cishou replied, "This may be called 'bringing forth a new intention within the bounds of formal law,' and 'entrusting wondrous principle beyond the realm of unrestrained brushwork. The Master said, "Does he understand Chan as well?"
Fodeng said, "I do not understand. The Duke asked, "Why do you not understand? Fodeng replied, "If I understood, I would not ask.
Thereupon, the Duke laughed heartily. Zheng Yugong of Xiaoxi, who studied the Way under Fodeng, also once spoke of this.
Yanyang Mountain lies forty *li* southeast of Wuning County.

There was a senior Dharma heir of the Venerable Master of Zhaozhou named Shanxin, who, delighting in the mountain’s extraordinary beauty, established a hermitage among its peaks. Xin was held in high esteem for his virtue and character.
The world did not wish to give him a name, so he was called Venerable Yan-yang. Two tigers and a snake would circle and dangle around his left and right sides.
The Venerable once asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when one brings nothing at all? Zhaozhou said, "Put it down.
The Venerable said, "Since I am bringing nothing at all, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou said, "If you cannot put it down..."
He then took it up and carried it away. Master Nanchan Huanglong had a verse to elucidate this, which says: "A single thing not brought forth, Cannot be lifted upon the shoulder.
Suddenly realizing one's error beneath the words, The heart is filled with boundless joy. Poisonous evil is cast from the mind."
Snakes and tigers became his intimate companions; several hundred years have passed since those days, yet the pure breeze has not ceased.
During the Tianyou era of the Tang dynasty, Liu Gong, the Regional Commander of Jiangxi, established Xinxing Monastery to the west of the county seat and invited the Venerable One to reside there.
A monk asked, "What is the water of Xinxing? He replied, "It is right before you in the river. Today, the name of the monastery has been changed.

To clarify the Mind: At the beginning of the dynasty, there was a monk named Daoning who wrote the verse on parting with the Venerable Master in the calligraphic style known as *fen-shu* (separated script) within the Hall of the Venerable One.
During the Daguan era, it still existed between the ruined walls, which read: "The body is like a cloud, the countenance is like the Patriarch;
When it comes to the body itself, there is no companion. Shouldering the crosier across my shoulder, I heed no one, And go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks."
Nowadays, monastic communities recite only the latter two lines, and they do not even know for whom they were composed.
That the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) has omitted the Venerable’s name is truly a cause for great lamentation.
Master Dahui was nineteen years old when, in the Dinghai year of the Daguang era, he passed through Taping Prefecture while traveling incognito.
While wandering with two monks at Beidu Hermitage, a dog bolted out and barked furiously. The two monks turned back in fear, but Dahui pressed straight forward.
The dog then greeted him as if welcoming a long-lost guest, and the abbot of the hermitage treated his encounter with exceptional hospitality. Dahui said: "I, [Name]..."
I, Jiawansheng, am but a person of late birth; how could I possibly be worthy of such great favor?

The abbot looked toward a clay statue in the monastery grounds and said, "Last night at about three o'clock, I dreamed that this man told me that today Chan Master Yunfeng Yue would arrive, and he instructed me to prepare for his reception.
Dahui declined, saying he was not clever enough. Upon returning to Yijing, he inquired of the elder monks about Yunfeng, and there were those who [could provide information].

The *Yunfeng Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Yunfeng) was presented for my inspection. Upon opening the volume, I felt a sense of sudden clarity; as I read through it, I recited it with sincerity and never forgot it.

From that time on, the monastic communities have transmitted the tradition that Dahuai was the reincarnation of Yunfeng. Upon his passing into *nirvāṇa*, there was once a memorial inscription for his spirit which stated briefly:
"The world knows him as the reincarnation of the Elder Yunfeng Yue; meeting the times, he obtained the former title of Nanyue Huairang. This is indeed so.
The Posthumous Title of National Teacher Nanyue Huairang was "Great Wisdom Chan Master" (Dahui Chanshi).
It is said that when National Teacher Nanyue resided at Jicui Hermitage on Mount Huangbo, Cheng Gongbei, the Regional Commander of Yuzhang, invited him to reside at Cuishan with a poem, saying:
"The springs and rocks of Cuishan crown the Western Mountains; I wish to have a Great Man dwell within these precincts. You were once already..."
The one who had been listening to the Dharma for years now wished once more to see his teacher’s countenance in this life. Nanhe said to him: "White hair fills your head like the Snow Mountains;

frail and weak, you lack the strength to leave the human world. Reflecting instead on how you have failed the commands of the lords and dukes, you wander in hesitation from dawn to dusk, only increasing your shame.
Two years passed after he returned to court, and he was again appointed as the Commissioner of Jiangxi. Nan sent him a verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
He said: "The great well was divided early, two years ago; the forest path and the official road are far apart. Recently I heard of the Bright Monarch’s decree from the Northern Gate;
you have again been appointed as the Acting Commissioner of Grain for Jiangxi. The various prefectures submit to your influence like grass bending before the wind;

my old friend can now rest his head high and sleep amidst the clouds. As for when I shall set out, I know not yet; I shall first entrust this letter to the messenger as a token of news. Cheng He replied:
He said: "Seven-character verses newly composed, recalling years past; at this time, my heart is filled with deep longing. You, Master, now possess the Way and dwell at the head of the Chan assembly;
as for me, what person am I to hold the power of an official? I often think of sitting beneath the clouds by the bright moon;

on the green mountains, I leave it to the sun to rise before I sleep. How many disciples are there before the hermitage? Those who come continue the tradition like a succession of lamps. — Cheng Zhi-shuai.

Yuzhang. This was in the third year of the Zhiping era, the Bingwu year. In accordance with the amnesty decree issued for the Mingtang ceremony, it was investigated and determined that monasteries not yet possessing official names should be granted them as a matter of precedent.
Consequently, all Vinaya monasteries within the jurisdiction of Yuzhang obtained their official titles. Today, few understand the underlying intent of this measure.
However, were it not for the fact that the Southern Master’s virtue and character were held in high esteem, how could they have received such external protection?
"Is the Dharma-gate thus diligent and earnest?
Liu Fangming of Chaoyang, while serving as the Governor of Kuifeng during the Shaoxing era, ascended the prefectural pavilion one night and saw a white light emanating from the ground.
He then dispatched men to investigate the location; it was found to be within the military camp's training field. At dawn, they excavated several feet.
After some time, he obtained a stone as large as a peck-measure (*dou*). He split it down the middle, and it was brilliantly pure with a circular mark.

Liu was delighted by this and composed a "Praise of the Auspicious Stone" (*Ruishi zan*), intending to carve it upon the surface. Just then, the Chan practitioner Jian passed by, and Liu informed him of his plan.
Jian replied, "Why not engrave a sacred image within the halo? This would cause people to gaze upon it in reverence; for such a radiance cannot be manifested except through a sacred image."
Thus it was. Liu was deeply impressed by these words and had the image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara painted by Li Bashi engraved.
At that time, the Great Master Dahui was residing in Hengyang; he was thus commissioned to compose a eulogy for it, saying:
"Neither cause nor condition, nor anything spontaneous—this stone and this painting are likewise so. This radiance is not contained within this physical form; this form does not arise from that."
Within this radiance, both are difficult to fathom with the intellect. The Great Being’s deliverance of sentient beings is likewise so. I have composed this verse to assist in its manifestation.
Those who contemplate it should purify their body, speech, and mind. Although the praise has been collected in the extensive records, its causal origin (*nidāna*) was omitted.
Thus, the full significance of his praise was not yet seen.
The Chief Administrator (Jian-si) Jingxun of Fengcheng and the Rector (Wei-na) Daoyi of Luling assisted Master Jiaozhong Guang of Quannan at his Dharma seat;
they were renowned throughout the rivers and lakes. Guang was a disciple of the great master Dahui, who was known as the "Zen Doctor of State" (Chan Zhuangyuan).

Zun possessed profound talent and refined intellect; his conversation was full of wit and flavor. Once, during the cold season at year’s end, while his friends were huddling around a brazier, Zun happened to be scratching a louse and playfully burned it on the fire.
Someone teased him, saying: "Duan Shizi was still able to compose a literary text to offer as a sacrifice to the cock that crows at dawn.
Since you, brother, have already burned the louse, how can you fail to deliver a Dharma discourse to ferry its spirit across?"
Xun spontaneously composed a verse, saying: "Listen to my words, you louse! From this day forward, you should take them to heart.
You have fallen among lice because of your greed for blood and flesh. You did not go to heaven to be born there, but instead came to life within my trousers.

You shall raise a son named 'The Nit. Those nits will be beyond counting, and my own body is not solid either; how could you possibly remain permanent? You must know that all is like a dream or an illusion."
This body is like lightning and like dew. I now open the skillful means to show you the place of transformation.
Within this single furnace, do not give rise to fear or terror. Exhaust this retributive body; do not follow the path of returning again. Ultimately, where will it be made to go?
Amidst a mass of blazing flames, with a single burst of sound, every dust mote and every world-system is without deviation. At this—
The friends were clamorous, declaring that he was far more virtuous than Duan Shizi Wen.
