In the summer of the first year of the Chongning era, the Venerable Jiyin was at Yungai in Changsha.

At that time, Lord Chen Guan (Yingzhong) had been banished to the regions beyond the Ling Mountains and sent a verse to him, requesting that he carry a copy of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra into the mountains. The verse said: [Verse omitted as per instructions]

The Great Being travels abroad; when his journey is ended, he returns. On the wind and moon of his home mountain, not a speck of dust remains. How many fields of leisure are upon the tip of his staff?
He carries the *Avataṃsaka* into the mountains. Jiyin harmonizes with this, saying: "Meeting by means of the Dharma, a smile breaks forth."
Looking down upon the world, it passes like drifting dust; do not distinguish between the shores of Lake Xiang and beyond the mountains.
Come and go together within the light of perfect stillness (*pariniṣpanna*). Thereafter, Jiyin (Huihong) incurred reprimand due to his association with the Master.
In the first year of the Jingkang era, he once presented a petition to the Ministry of Justice, stating: "The suspended monk Huihong, currently aged fifty-six, is a native of Junzhou. Yuan...

He was a monk registered at Xiangji Monastery on the Right Street. Previously, during the early Chongning era, the censor Chen Guan had remonstrated against Cai Jing’s affairs and incurred imperial displeasure, resulting in his exile to Lianzhou.

Because Huìhóng perceived that Chen Guan had fulfilled his duty with integrity and had been cast into the southern seas, traveling ten thousand *li* alone, he feared that the latter might fall into negligence or hardship;
thus, he went back and forth across the sea to provide for him before and after [the journey].
For four years, he was on intimate terms with Chen Guan (Chen Guàn). Furthermore, it was through this connection that he obtained ordination as a monk;

his name had originally been submitted for recommendation by the late Chancellor Zhang Shangying (Zhang Shāngyīng). In the first year of the Zhènghé era, Zhang Shangying petitioned to obtain the *Zūnyáo lù* (Record of Honoring Yao) composed by Chen Guan.
At that time, the eunuch Liáng Shíchéng was colluding with Cài [Jìng], and seeing that the Chancellor was recommending Cài Jìng, [he sought to suppress] Chen [Guan], his enemy.
Chen Guàn employed every possible stratagem to undermine and entrap him. Within a mere month, he was indeed expelled.
Suspecting that Huihóng had provided cover for Chen Guàn, [the authorities] grew incensed and urged Li Xiàoshòu, the Governor of Kaifeng, to arrest Huihóng and throw him into prison.

He was subjected to unjust interrogation and specifically sentenced to exile at Jiyang Commandery. Later, due to illness and being unable to endure forced labor, he was granted imperial favor and released to go into retirement.

It has now been fourteen years since then. Recently, I have heard that the imperial court has posthumously conferred official ranks and titles upon Zhang Shangying and Chen Guan to honor their loyalty and integrity, while banishing Cai Jing and Liang Shicheng to the southern frontier to rectify their crimes.
This clearly demonstrates that the circumstances of my own former imprisonment were indeed grievous and unjust. I, Huìhóng, have personally observed that during the Shaosheng era in Hangzhou...

The monk Daoqian was on intimate terms with the Imperial Secretary Su Shi. His enemy Lü Shengqing, serving as the Commissioner of the Western Circuit of Zhejiang, arrested Daoqian and handed him over to the Suzhou prison.

Through judicial corruption, he was sentenced to administrative exile in Yanzhou. Later, after the matter was reviewed and cleared by the imperial court, his status was rectified and he was reinstated as a monk.
Recently, I encountered the monk Yongdao of the Right Street; in the early years of the Xuanhua era, he had been converted into a *deshi* (Daoist priest).
I submitted a memorial to plead for his rescue. The Prefect of Kaifeng, Sheng Zhang, arrested him and sentenced him to penal servitude in Daozhou.
Fortunately, within last year, he was granted a pardon. I reflect deeply that Huìhóng committed no other offense;

it was solely because the officials of Kaifeng, looking to the power of the Inner Court eunuchs, unjustly administered the law against him. His grievance and the circumstances of the case are identical to those of Dàoqián and Yǒngdào.

The preceding and succeeding cases were identical. Now, having come forward with a formal petition to the Minister of the Department of State Affairs, I wish to request that, following the precedent of Daoqian and Yongdao, he be granted a special correction of his status to become a monk. Fearing to act on my own authority, I humbly await Your Majesty’s decree.
At that time, however, the affairs of the court were beset by many complications, and the matter was not carried out. Yet in the summer of the following year, Jiyin passed away at Mount Tong.
Peace. Han She-ren Zicang composed an inscription for his stupa, stating that "his friend Xian invited resentment. This is indeed a statement that knows the truth.
*Yunwo Jitan*, Volume Upper;
*Yunwo Jitan*, Volume Lower.
The Master of Pure Wisdom (Jingzhi Dashi), Huiguang, the incumbent of Miaohui Nunnery in the Eastern Capital, was born into the Fan family of Chengdu.

His written work is titled *Tangjian* (Mirror of the Tang), and he was the uncle of [the author]. During the reign of Emperor Hui, the imperial palace bestowed Dharma robes upon various senior Chan masters;
Huiguang was among those so honored. Consequently, he was commanded to preach the Dharma according to his rank, and Huiguang received his turn accordingly.
At the conclusion, he ascended the seat. After the exchange of questions and answers was finished, he looked out over the assembly and said:

"As for discussing Zen or speaking of the Way, the great Zen masters of the past have already spoken on these matters. What could this mountain monk say here? Have you not seen what the former sages said:
'A thousand kinds of words, ten thousand varieties of explanations—these are only intended to ensure that you remain forever undeluded'? Since it is thus,"
"Is it so? After all, how is it? Guang then covered his head with his dharma robe. After a long while, he said, "The patched robe covers the head, and all matters cease;
at this moment, even this mountain monk understands nothing. He then descended from the seat. On that day, the assembly of monastics and laypeople who listened numbered in the tens of thousands.
There was no one who did not sigh in admiration and submit. Thus, Han She-ren Zicang inscribed the epitaph for Guang’s stupa, extolling his vast learning and skillful eloquence.
The stupa was established at the site of the Sacred Image on Mount Xi in Yuzhang.
Formerly, when Emperor Zong was presiding at Zhonghua Palace, he composed the "Discourse on the Examination of the 'On the Origin of the Way'":

"I have observed that regarding Han Yu’s 'On the Origin of the Way,' there has been no one yet capable of distinguishing how Buddhism and Daoism are conflated and how the Three Teachings mutually contradict one another.
Furthermore, its prose is prolix and its principles are circuitous; when measured against the mind of the Sage, it is not yet clear. Why is this? Because the Śākya school..."
Exhausting one's life and destiny, casting aside the physical form, and not clinging to names or appearances, one naturally has no concern with worldly affairs;

how much less, then, would one be involved with rites, music, benevolence, or righteousness? Nevertheless, he still established the precepts: do not kill, do not commit sexual misconduct, do not steal, do not drink alcohol, and do not speak falsely.
Now, not killing is benevolence (*ren*); not committing sexual misconduct is propriety (*li*); not stealing is righteousness (*yi*); and not drinking alcohol—
This is knowledge. Not speaking falsely is faith. If one approaches Zhongni (Confucius) in this manner, how could he be far away?
The Master moves with ease within the Middle Way; he is a sage. What the sage does—what is not ritual and music? What is not benevolence and righteousness? How then could one name it [otherwise]?
It is like the movement of heaven and earth, the circulation of yin and yang without beginning or end; how could there be any intentional "spring"?

The distinctions between summer, autumn, winter, and spring are merely what the sages have given them as provisional names. This is also like the distinctions between ritual, music, benevolence, and righteousness;

it is because the sages established these teachings to govern the world that they could not help but do so. If one examines these provisional names and seeks their source, they are found to be the Dao.
The Dao is the ultimate source of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music. Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music are, in truth...
This is the function of the Way. Yang Xiong claimed that the Master of Lao [Laozi] "hammered away at benevolence and righteousness" and "extinguished ritual and music.
Yet, if we now examine the traces of Laozi’s own writings, those he treasures are threefold: namely, compassion (*ci*), frugality (*jian*), and not daring to take precedence over the world.
Confucius said, "Gentleness, kindness, reverence, frugality, and yielding," and further stated, "Only benevolence (*ren*) is great. Is what Laozi calls compassion not precisely this?
"Is this not the greatest form of benevolence? [The other] replied, "I dare not take precedence over all under heaven. Is this not the greatest form of humility?
When it comes to their convergence upon the Way, each school emphasizes one aspect; what they value is purity, stillness, and unity. Are they therefore truly at odds with the Sage Confucius?
It is merely that those of the later generations of the Three Teachings, being ignorant, cling to these differences and treat them as distinct. Indeed, as for Buddhism and Daoism...
To sever discursive thought and abide in non-action is simply to cultivate the mind and body.
Confucius’s teaching on governing the world differs only in its application; it is like using a plow for weaving or a loom for plowing.

Those of later generations have merely been confused by this clamor, and thus they have surely lost the underlying principle. Someone asks: "How should one eliminate this confusion? I reply: "Cultivate the mind through the Buddha."
To govern the self through Laozi’s teachings and to govern the world through Confucianism—this is appropriate. Only a sage is able to unify these two;
thus, they must not fail to be discussed.
As for Chan Master Xian, during the Xining era, Zhang Gongjian, the Governor of Luling, commissioned him to take up the abbacy at Longqing Monastery. Not long after...
After one year, Wang Gongshao led him to Mount Longquan in Western Mountain in Yuzhang. Not more than a year later, he declined his duties due to illness.
The monastics and laypeople of Luling prepared a boat to welcome him back to Longqing, where he was lodged in the West Hall.

After two years and two seasons had passed, on the thirteenth day of the third month of the fourth year of the Yuanfeng era, he left behind this verse: "The physical form floats in the world; suddenly the physical form floats away into extinction."

At the age of fifty-three, during the sixth, seventh, and eighth months at Mount Nanyue and Mount Tiantai, amidst the pines and winds and the snow in the mountain streams, he bid farewell to his fellow seekers.
Amidst a glowing brazier, a *utpala* flower appeared; he then sat peacefully until his passing. He had an artist come to paint his true likeness, whereupon his head suddenly raised itself on its own.
The following day, he continued to gaze steadily. His recorded sayings had only reached a few sections when they were published in Southern Fujian (Quannan).

There was a question posed during his formal teaching session (*shishō*) that said: "What inscription does the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs bear? How deep or shallow is the source of all Buddhas? He further asked:
"Throughout the twelve periods of the day, as you come and go, opening your bedding and unfolding your bowl—this is merely a body composed of the five aggregates subject to decay.
Which one, then, is the pure *dharmakāya*? He said again, "Do not point east or draw west; bring forth a single phrase from the ground of reality.
He said yet again, "In the twelve periods of the day, when putting on clothes and eating food, by whose grace and power do you receive these things?"
It is said: "When the fish swims, the water becomes turbid; when the bird flies, feathers fall. Once Master Liang entered the Western Mountains, why was there no further news?
The wondrous signs of his cremation are detailed in the record by Su Shi (Huangmen Ziyou).
Therefore, I have here briefly recorded his final verses and his parting instructions, so that their true substance may not perish.
The Master of Bajiao Hermitage on Mount Nanyue was commonly called Grand Master Quan, as his songs and verses occasionally took "The Great Way" (Dàdào) as their title.
For example, his verse on the "Six Bar-noses" says: "The bar-nose of the Great Way—when questioned, he is dozing; on his back, he carries a gourd."

Mad songs and unrestrained play: the nostrils of the "scattered sages" (*san sheng*). Performing as the occasion demands, surging east and submerging west, throughout the southern provinces and northern villages:
the nostrils of the *chan* masters. Whether gain or loss, the towering heights of the emerald peaks; dragon-like gait and tiger-like gaze: the nostrils of the patch-robed monks (*nàsēng*).
The sitting mat is twelve feet square; cease seeking its length or breadth. When the wind is high and clouds arise, the Master of the Seat reveals his true essence.

His eloquence flows like a rushing river without obstruction; golden lotuses spring from the earth. With hands holding the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel), the mountain boy reveals his own essence. Gold is tested with fire; a guest asks about dwelling in the mountains.
"It is no easy matter to have traveled so far. One day, he composed a wild song, saying: "A-he-he!
I remember last year in Qingzhou, Eating a jujube fruit. Now, standing here, I suddenly reflect; Laughing alone and singing alone, I let myself go."
Zhang Dian, Li Babo, Huangpo, and Zheng Jiuxiao—how restless their minds! They lose the great cat from the head of the bed and run out the gate to catch a toad.
Stop searching further! Clouds from the southern mountain draw in clouds from the northern mountain;
go back, return! One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Though these words seem unrestrained, their essential meaning has a point of return.
Since he considered himself content, he was more than sufficient to illuminate the monastic community.

At the Prajñā Hermitage in Min County, Fuzhou, during the Jiayin year of the Shaoxing era, there was the Elder Naidong Jiang Daibei Xian, who was eighty-four years old at the time. While Master Dahui resided at Yangyu, he [interacted] with the Prajñā [community].
Separated by only a single stream, Xian remained diligent in his investigation despite his advanced age. Recently, he had been entering the room for private instruction with the assembly.
Dahui asked him, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Xian replied, "One who cannot be supported.
Dahui said, "Who is it that cannot be supported? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As Xian was about to respond, Dahui struck him with a bamboo staff.
As soon as he struck him with the comb, Xian was suddenly enlightened. Dahuì praised him with a verse, saying: "One blow shatters the cave of birth and death;
at that moment, both ordinary and sage are cut off from their tracks. I laugh instead at Zhaozhou, whose mind never rested, still wandering east and west even in his old age.
There was one in Min who mocked him with a verse, saying: "An eighty-year-old old man performing the 'idle' consecration, speaking only of..."
Nowadays the road is difficult to travel; amidst the misty waves at the ocean gate and the offshore islets, the old fisherman still holds his fishing rod.
Dahui composed four verses on this, saying: An eighty-year-old elder performs the *abhiṣeka* in leisure; The king of geese knows how to choose the milk for himself.
I send word to the blind lacquer buckets of the monasteries: do not mistake the cry of a crane for the song of a nightingale. It is only said that the road is difficult to travel these days;
three times three before, and three times three after. I send word to the blind lacquer buckets of the monasteries: let go at the head of the clouds and come back to study.
Amidst the misty waves of the ocean’s entrance and its islands, how many people have actually reached within? I send word to the monasteries...
Blind lacquer bucket! There is no need to give rise to greed or anger behind one's back. As before, the old fisherman holds his fishing rod; the jeweled scales, shrimp, and crabs are not overlooked.
I send word to the blind lacquer buckets of the monastic groves: do not regard the meditation topic in terms of arising and ceasing.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, Chan Master Foyin traveled from Guizong on Mount Lu to accept an invitation to Jinshan.
While his boat was moored at Qinzhun, he went to visit Lord Wang (Wang Anshi) at Dinglin. Lord Wang requested a eulogy for a portrait of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) from Shuanglin.
Foyin took up his brush and wrote: "The Way is the cap, the Confucianism the shoes, and the Buddha the monastic robe; harmonizing these three schools into one."
The family has forgotten the path to the Tuṣita Heaven; they sit in delusion by the Twin Śāla Trees awaiting the Dragon Flower Assembly.

Although you, Master, were exhorted by Foyin, you ultimately submitted to the profundity of his words and reasoning; thus, you wrote several hundred characters of the *Maitreya-praṇidhāna-gāthā* in a small hand as a response.
Huang Tingjian (Shanggu) provided the colophon. Since Foyin resided at Yunju, this was engraved upon stone. Furthermore—
He remains [in the records].
The Elder Huayan of Weifeng was named Huaidong. During the Five Dynasties period, he initially propagated the teachings of the Avatamsaka Sutra.

Later, he studied under Chan Master Xinghua Cunzong, whereupon he attained the essence of the "special transmission outside the teachings. He subsequently appeared in the world at Tianbo Monastery and later moved to...
In the Chan garden of Ya-sha, the monastics and laypeople of the Hexi region revered him; thus he was called "Old Huayan.
He is the one mentioned in the *Chanmen Zongpai Tu* (Chart of the Lineages of the Chan School) as Tianbo Heshang, whose lineage descended from Xinghua. Dong once addressed the assembly, saying:
The Buddha-Dharma is present in your daily activities; it is present in your walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; in your drinking tea and eating rice;
in your speaking and questioning one another; and in all that you do. Yet, if you raise a thought or stir a single mental movement, it is no longer so. Do you understand?
If you were to understand this, you would be a person bearing a cangue and shackles, burdened by heavy transgressions. Why is this so?
The Buddha-dharma is not far away; though separated by kalpas as numerous as dust motes and sands, it can be seen within a single thought-moment, right upon your eyebrows and nostrils.
If you cannot see it, it is like trying to reach the moon by joining bamboo poles together—it is impossible. Have you realized this to the end?
Do not contemplate at all; it cannot be expressed in words. At this very moment, by what power of grace do you sustain yourself? If you can know this, there must be a place of joy.
Therefore, the ancients said: "In profound stillness, there is constant clarity; the Buddhas do not seek it out, and sentient beings have cut off all news.
Do you understand yet? All Buddhas are fundamentally without sentiment; all Buddhas are fundamentally without [discrimination].
[This is] the name. All sentient beings are fundamentally numinous from the beginning; they are as indistinctly vast as great empty space, lacking nothing and having no excess.
If you do not understand this, you will inevitably encounter obstructions wherever you go. Now, the *Línjiān lù* attributes this to the words of Master Tiānbō Yuán.
Furthermore, it is an error to claim that Yuan was an elder of the Huayan school. Yuan succeeded Tianyi Hui; he was the fifth-generation descendant of Yunmen.
Yuan regarded Linji as his grandfather, and the essential purport of his preaching can certainly be verified accordingly.
The Dharma-person Wujie was the daughter of Official Zhang Yuan Dao; the Dharma-person Chaozong was the mother of the younger brother of Official Liu Jigao.
Both had received the prediction of enlightenment at the gate of the Great Master Dahui.
Once, Wujie went to Jing Mountain to sweep the pagoda, composing a verse that said: "The robes are damp with the tears of Vulture Peak; the incense burner burns the fragrance of Shaoshi."
Clouds and mountains fill the void before my eyes; I do not see the King of the Dharma. At that time, Chaozong did not arrive, and Wujie urged him to come.
Chaozong replied with a verse: "The stupa is originally free of dust; why use a broom to sweep it? Sweeping would only give rise to more dust; that is why I have not arrived.
Formerly, when Wujie was still living at home, a physiognomist passed by him and said, "This is a person who shall sit upon a precious throne to preach the Dharma."
Later, she indeed became a nun, named Huizhao. In her later years, she succeeded her tonsure master, Fazhou Wuzhuo, at his dharma seat.
She once praised Chan Master Yuanwu with a *Yujia'ao* (Fisherman’s Delight) verse: "Seven times he sat upon the site of enlightenment, Three times he received imperial summons.
When will these empty flowers and water-moons end? Within the sound of the little jade bell, he realized the Way— Truly laughable! From the beginning, he has deceived us in vain."
What fine descendants! His eloquence surged like the sound of the ocean tide, vast and rolling; his clarity was like the bright moon shining from the sky.

As he traveled westward with his flying staff, the clouds stretched into the distance. The gibbons of Ba cried out; everyone sang along to the tune of returning home. In the seventh year of the Qiandao era, he moved to reside at Mingyin Temple in Linping.
On the sixth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Chunxi era, he suddenly took leave of his son, Liang Qian, at Wuyi Commandery.
The verdict was passed. He went directly to Kuangxiao Monastery and passed away while sitting upon his meditation seat. When his hair was shorn, countless *śarīra* relics were found.

Although it was the height of the scorching summer, he remained in his quarters for several days with his countenance solemn and unchanged. Juezhen, a junior disciple who had resided at Zishou Monastery, escorted him back to Gusu.

They temporarily enshrined him on Mount Lengqia for eleven autumns; subsequently, his son moved the remains back to Sangu. As soon as the reliquary casket emerged from its niche, a spring [began to flow].
The water surged upward accordingly, causing both the monastics and the laity to be struck with awe and reverence. Is this not a manifestation of the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
As for Master Zheng: he was the son of the Huang family of Huating. At only five years of age, upon seeing Buddhist scriptures, he was able to point out and recognize their characters;

as soon as he was prompted to read them, he would recite them fluently and clearly. By the time he reached adulthood, he entered Zisheng Monastery on Mount Beishan in Hangzhou to take up residence under a master.

The essence of the matter is fundamentally suchness. Zhu Shaonan, a man of the commandery, wished to offer his treasury gold to restore the monastic registers, but [the Master] shook his head and did not consent.
He then said with regret: "In antiquity, the conferring of ordination was based on clear spiritual capacity and profound understanding; nowadays it is quite otherwise.

It is simply a matter of discarding the elderly and the young, making their heads bald and their bodies clad in coarse cloth. Alas, how can the true ever overcome the false? The world is full of such [deceptions]."
Is this so? Before long, he was graced by the profound and generous bestowal of the *xiangfu* (auspicious talisman) honors, yet he alone continued to wear his tattered woolen robe.
His colleagues looked down upon him, but Zheng said: "As for the Buddha, the Buddha—does it lie in his physical appearance? As for a monk, a monk—does it lie in his fine garments?"
Thereafter, someone offered to provide the annual expenditures for maintenance so that he might continue with the affairs of the monastery; however, he declined, saying:

"I have heard of begging for alms while walking, but never of sitting at ease to enjoy offerings. I have heard of visiting various patriarchs one after another, but never of neglecting study to take on responsibilities.

Furthermore, my age is still young and my vigor intact; this is precisely the time when one should exert physical strength in performing ritual services, rather than being occupied with the management of buildings."

It was autumn. Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled east, studying the Three Contemplations at Tiantai. He then returned to Mount Jing, where he consulted with the elder Jusu regarding the principle of the Single Transmission.
Subsequently, he attended upon Jusu and served him while managing the Pure Land Temple on Mount Gongchen in Lin’an.
He exerted himself in unison to organize all affairs. During the Tianxi era, Jusu passed away, and Zheng followed the consensus of the assembly to succeed him on the seat.
Zheng Ya was rich in learning; his poetry possessed the spirit of Tao Qian and Xie Lingyun. When practicing the calligraphy of Wang Xizhi and Xie Hun, he further esteemed simplicity and purity.

As for his outstanding discourses, he was esteemed as a preeminent master of erudition and eloquence. Even such figures as Wang Wenkang, Xu Neihan, Wu Xuandian, and Cai Mixue all delighted in engaging with him in excursions beyond the mundane world (*fangwai*).
Nevertheless, in his daily life, his discernment and contemplation were clear and untroubled, remaining free from worldly entanglements.

Though burdened by the world, he maintained a pure and noble character, which is especially evident in his poetry. A *gāthā* on walking along a stream says: "A single bend of the small stream, and a poem is complete;
Drinking in the very source of poetry, the lines grow ever clearer. Reaching the upper reaches, I rest awhile in stillness; Clouds part and mist breaks, as the moon shines bright.
On the eighth day of the first month of summer in the first year of the Huangyou era, he addressed the assembly, saying: "As for movement, it exists in response to..."
"Quiescence has never had a limit. I have been active for sixty-four years; now I am at rest.
Yet, in the ultimate sense, what is there of either activity or stillness? Thereupon, he passed away in profound serenity.
When National Teacher [Huangbo] resided at Huangbo Mountain, he composed five stanzas of verse in response to the Elder Zou. They read as follows: "Short prefaces and long letters are all elegant;

The five-character and seven-character lines require further effort. If you can ensure that word and deed constantly attend to one another, For ten thousand ages you shall be a new Confucian gentleman of Xinchang.
The second stanza says: "Days pass and months come like the casting of a shuttle; One does not realize that the face and years are silently consumed. I urge you..."
May you swiftly tread the path to Bodhi; do not concern yourself excessively with the clamor of worldly conventions. Third: At this time, the minds of men are overgrown with weeds;
because of their karmic retribution, they have lost their way. Whether monk or layperson, throughout the world, one must ensure that one’s words accord with one’s deeds. Fourth:
For a long time I have heard that you are fond of vegetarianism and the recitation of sutras, and I admire how the lotus flower grows within the fire. Floating...
The world’s toil and labor are all but dreams and illusions. My earnest exhortation is simply this: it is your true future path. (5) Fifth:

This servant speaks of returning and shall not dwell here for long; I have composed these few verses in response to your letter. Having fortunately found the mists and clouds as neighbors, from now on we shall know one another, and virtue shall not be solitary.
Master Nanchan replied with a *gāthā* to inquire after his health and well-being; such an exchange may truly be called "even in moments of haste."
He did not forget the guidance on the Path.
Professor Yan Gong Chaokang of Raozhou sought the Way from Xuedang at Jianfu Monastery; Baen’s Ying’an once offered a verse which said:
"Zhaozhou says the dog has no Buddha-nature; I say the dog has Buddha-nature. Suddenly he spoke—

Below, he realized for himself where he was headed. From this point on, he no longer believed the words of Zhaozhou; he applied his spirit and exerted himself. To follow behind others is not the way of a master;
to ride a cow while searching for the cow is enough to make people laugh to death. Only now has he finally realized that all his previous efforts were in vain.
At that time, the Great Master Dahui was at Mei Yang. Yan sent him this verse, and Dahui replied with a letter, which stated in brief:
"Following behind others leaves no room for skillful hands; these eighty-four thousand [teachings] are all public pathways.
Yan was a native of Changxing in Huzhou.
Master Wenshu Dao of Dingzhou initially traveled to the lecture halls of Chengdu, where he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi lun) for nearly several decades.

Someone challenged him, saying, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Now, with all these things standing densely before our eyes, where is the mind and consciousness?
Dao was at a loss and did not know how to respond. He then left the gorges and traveled throughout the Yangtze and Huai regions.

Eventually, he arrived at Taiping in Shu, where he heard that Chan Master Fojian was giving a night discourse on Zhaozhou’s story of the cypress tree in the courtyard. When the discourse reached Master Jue’s words...
My former teacher did not say this, which left me in great doubt. After reflecting upon it for a long time, one night it suddenly dawned upon me.
I expressed this realization in verse, saying: "Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree; Zen practitioners have passed it down throughout the world.
Most merely pluck at the leaves and seek among the branches, Unable to understand directly from the very source. Master Jue says he never spoke these words— This is precisely [the truth]."
"Malicious words and face-to-face insults—if a Zen practitioner possesses the eye that penetrates all quarters, they should skillfully discern the true from the false within them.
When Fojiàn passed away at Zhōngshān, [Changlu Zongze] offered incense while expressing his grief, saying: "Sorrowfully recalling this year’s tenth month, the eighth day..."
At Mount Zhong, the former Master entered nirvana; the stone woman wailed in grief at their parting. From the eyes of the wooden man, tears flowed like blood.
How profound was the sentiment of the path between teacher and disciple! Each time I recall him, I am choked with sobs.
I rely only upon this single incense stick of purple sandalwood to honor what he said—or did not say—those years ago. It is said that he lived to the age of seventy-two. During the Jiyan era...
On the Shangsi day of the You month, he was killed by the great rebel of Hunan, Zhong Xiang. The Abbot of Dianniu, Master You, lamented him in verse:

I wish to borrow thirty *kè* of the night’s window-light to sit cross-legged upon a *húcháng* and investigate the fluttering of the banner in the wind.

If one gazes intently yet does not see, is it not because of the karmic obstruction of their eyes? For those who possess true knowledge and vision are rare;

All emerge from the Dharma-body of the Great Being. Ma Tian’s offering was praised by Dongpo; those who beheld it were innumerable, and all attained Buddhahood.

I have humbly received your gracious instruction regarding the *Qingliang* and the *Linji* school’s public cases as expounded by Master Li. The principles and phenomena are clearly elucidated;
who would dare raise dissent? Alas, this man of unfinished business has been thoroughly exposed all at once by Master Wujin.
Although his offense shall not be severely punished and his past shall not be held against him, he still remains subject to thirty blows for his lack of sincerity.
A blow! If you act strictly according to the command, it appears all the more that the Dharma is exhausted and there are no subjects.
If you allow even a single thread of leniency, I fear they will knowingly commit transgressions. Between these two paths, how can one be correct?
That superior man is difficult to answer; one can only retreat three thousand li. As stated in the separate letter, this is the full extent of my intention. Your kindness remains sealed separately.
He showed it to Wujin. Wujin wrote a verse on a plain sheet of paper enclosed in a seal and sent it to En, saying:
"There is no need to run three thousand li backward; why must you again inflict thirty strokes of the bamboo? All is a true treasure-trove as vast as the sands of the Ganges;
when the night grows cold, lift up the lamp for reading. En then composed four verses in response, which began: "There is no need to run three thousand..."
The vast, clear waves roll across the level ground; atop the hundred-foot pole, one laughs without ceasing. Linji and Deshan stand by, their ears pricked;
why need one again administer thirty blows of the staff? Letting go or holding fast—this is the reliance. That the Layman has transmitted it must surely remain;
the Three Peaks stand like tripods, their blue ridges layer upon layer. All are true treasuries of the sands of the Ganges, offered here as a gift to people.
In the intervals between activities, I returned home. Upon my arrival, I had no words to ask Lu Neng; I was struck with wonder at the "clay ox swallowing a great elephant.
The night was cold as I lit the lamp for reading; an old monk with a tattered robe covering his head.
How shameful that Vimalakīrti possessed such great spirit, while I, pitying myself, am plagued by illness and utterly incapable. This is the disciple of Master Qing of Touzishan.
Dharma Master Yongdao was born into the Mao clan of Shenqiu in Dongying. He took An Gong, a monk of Nanluohan Monastery in Shunchang Prefecture, as his teacher.
Subsequently, he lamented, saying: "The Buddha established the teachings to extensively deliver all classes of beings.
If I do not now protect the gates of the Dharma and strive to investigate the Mahayana for the benefit of sentient beings, my efforts will be in vain. Thereupon, he proceeded to the capital.

At the *dujiang* (lecturer’s seat), he specialized in the two treatises of *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*, reaching their profound depths. He subsequently presided over Xiangji Temple in the Left Street (*zuo-jie*).
On the occasion of the Tianning Festival, by imperial decree, he received the honorary title of Master Baojue.

In the first month of the first year of the Xuande era, an edict was issued to change the designation of monks to "virtuous practitioners" (*deshi*). [He was joined by] Vinaya Master Wuming and Huayan Lecturer Hui... (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
One day, he debated the nature of heterodoxy and orthodoxy with the Daoist Lin Lingsu and petitioned the imperial court on the matter. Having offended the Emperor’s will, he was exiled to Daozhou.

In the sixth month of the second year, he was transferred to a less severe location by imperial amnesty; while passing through Changsha, he encountered the Venerable Jiyin and sent him a poem, saying:
"Master Dao's courage is greater than his own frame, Daring to scale the dragon's scales to submit a remonstrance. He desires only to bare..."
Shouldering the Buddha-dharma, he willingly extended his neck to endure the axe and hoe. For three years in exile, his heart was free of shame;

returning ten thousand *li* away, his countenance showed no witheredness. It is recently heard that those who serve as the pillars of the teaching’s discipline now follow the court with their ceremonial boots and tablets.
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the seventh year, by imperial decree: "The former Master Baoguo, Mao Yongdao, has repeatedly undergone amnesties."
He was pardoned and granted special permission to resume his monastic tonsure according to former custom. From then on, he repeatedly received imperial favors.

Not long after, at the beginning of the Jianyan era, the Generalissimo stationed in the capital, Lord Zong—who was clothed in virtue, morality, and righteousness—ordered him to be provisionally appointed as a *Xuanchiao Lang* (Imperial Instructor) to serve as the Commissioner for Persuasion and Adjutant General for the Office of the Imperial Resident, tasked with assisting the military command and dispatched to Huai and Ying.

He exhorted the wealthy and influential to contribute tens of thousands of coins to assist the state and provision the army. He was repeatedly summoned to attend court and deliberate on affairs at the Imperial Itinerary Hall (Xingzai Dutang).

Thereupon, the high officials and ministers earnestly urged him to return. Initially, he was appointed to a civil office while concurrently holding a military rank, tasked with commanding military forces to aid the royal house.
He then composed a verse to decline the offer, saying: "In years past, for the sake of the Dharma, I suffered the branding of my face. Heaven...
Appointed as a supervisor to oversee the military, I was imprisoned and sent south for half a decade. Traveling ten thousand *li* back and forth, I calculated the journey’s length;
yet amidst frost and ice, my integrity remained as firm as pine and bamboo, and amidst glowing coals, my resolve stayed as unyielding as iron and stone.

I wish only to become a disciple of the Buddha; I am unfit to serve as a high minister or official. Although these words are not refined, they merely record the facts. This was subsequently submitted for approval by the Three Departments.

A Memorandum from the Office for Rewarding Merit of the Secretariat: We have received an Imperial Decree specifically granting the title of *Bǎojiào Yuántōng Fǎjì Dàshī* (Great Master of Precious Enlightenment, Perfect Penetration, and Dharma Aid).

The official document from the Ministry of Rites states: "Regarding the aforementioned monastic title, according to the laws of our ancestors, it corresponds to the rank of Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Hónglù Qīng*).
Following the Chóngguān era, six-character titles were established; these are ranked according to the civil officials. Furthermore, this has been approved by the Central Secretariat."
An official memorandum was issued to honor his protection of the Dharma, and he was granted the name Fadao.

In the second month of the third year of the Shaoxing era, he went to the imperial court together with the Daoist Liu Ruqian and others to rectify the seating order for monks and Daoists at the sites of prayer and ritual. The memorandum stated in brief:
During the Chongning and Daguan eras, Daoist practitioners such as Wang Zixi and Lin Lingsu arrogantly usurped official ranks, thereby throwing the imperial administration into disorder.

Consequently, a precedent was established whereby the Daoist order was ranked above the monastic community. I have observed that since the Jingkang and Jianyan periods, all official titles and stipends held by Daoists have been rescinded.
As they no longer possess the protection of official rank, they ought to revert to following the ancient traditions of our ancestors.
I respectfully request that the Court issue a clear decree to grant a special correction and promulgate it throughout the realm to rectify social customs.

At that time, however, no final decision was reached for implementation. It was not until the tenth month of the thirteenth year of the Shaoxing era that the seating order for monks and Daoists was once again standardized:
monks were to sit to the east, which became the permanent regulation. In the seventh month of the seventeenth year, the Daoists...
On the twenty-seventh day, he passed away at the Xiangfu Hermitage in Lin’an Prefecture. His verse on departing this world says: "The myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty;
the single reality is devoid of delusion. It is like that great void, originally identical to the echo in the valley.

As for the *Dongdu Shilüe* (Abridged History of the Eastern Capital), it states that the Daoist Lin Lingsu gained favor through heterodox ways, his influence eclipsing that of his time. Yet, as for the Way and—
In his vigorous debate, he was entirely without a word of retreat. His protection of the Dharma-gate and his benefit to sentient beings truly do not belie his original vow.

The world has mistakenly taken "Upāsaka" (伊蒲塞) to mean "offering of pond-plants and algae" (蘋藻); this must surely be a long-standing convention that has never been examined. Now, observing the East...

From the "Biography of Ying, Prince of Chu" in the *Book of Han*: In the eighth year of the Yongping era, an imperial decree was issued ordering that all those facing the death penalty throughout the empire might redeem their lives by offering silk.

Ying dispatched the Commandant of the Imperial Secretaries to present thirty bolts of yellow silk and white gauze to the Regional Inspector, saying: "I am entrusted with the position of a vassal protector."
As his transgressions accumulated, he joyfully received the Heavenly Grace; he offered silk fabrics to redeem his sins and offenses.
The Chancellor reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict in reply, saying: "The King of Chu expounds the subtle words of Huang-Lao and honors the benevolent temples of the Buddha.

Having purified himself for three months, he has made a vow with the spirits. What cause for suspicion or doubt could there be that he would constantly harbor regrets and offenses? Let the ransom silks be returned to him, so as to assist him."
"Upāsaka-sramaṇa-śreṣṭha-bhojana. Its commentary states: "Upāsaka" is the same as "upāsaka," which in the Middle Kingdom (China) is translated as "near-dweller" (*upavāsa*).
This refers to one who has received the precepts and is thus fit to dwell near the Sangha; by this it can be seen that [the offering] is not merely wild greens and algae.
Furthermore, *sāman* is the same as *śramaṇa*, translated as "one who has stilled the mind. The *Śūranāma-sūtra* states:

"Because one quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source, one is called a śramaṇa. Now, in the land of India, there are five such destinations, and due to regional dialects, the pronunciations differ.
As for the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, and upāsikā, these are known as the fourfold assembly (*catur-parṣad*). Having prepared an abundant feast, [he...]
If one is hosting a feast, it would also be acceptable to refer to it as a "vegetarian meal for the fourfold assembly.
Chan Master Jinshan Daguan Ying was a man of extraordinary character and refined spirit; his intellect was sharp and subtle, and there was no scripture or history that he had not studied.
His literary compositions were likewise elegant and refined. He associated with Xia Yinggong, Wang Wengkanggong, Ouyang Wenzhonggong, and Zhao Canzheng Pingshu;

they took great pleasure in each other’s company. He once composed the "Discourse on Nature" (*Xingbian*), stating: "Regarding those who have discussed nature among the sages and worthies of antiquity and the present..."
This can only be understood through the mind. Even if one is able to exhaustively investigate principle (*li*), if one cannot fully realize nature (*xing*), why is this?

It is because one does not know that the Three Powers (*sancai*) and the myriad things are all nature itself. From the nature of Heaven above to the nature of Humanity below: metal is sharp, water is moist, wood is straight, fire is hot, and earth is substantial—these are the natures of the Five Elements (*wuxing*).
If one discusses them collectively and examines them with precision, the natures of the myriad things are clearly visible.
Among these, the most spiritual is humanity. Born from the union of yin and yang, that which undergoes transformation and movement is emotion (*qing*).
To restrain human emotion is to restore its original purity. It is by this means that one may rise or fall, become a sage or a fool.
Those whose innate nature (*xing*) is superior are the *junzi*; their external emotions cannot delude their nature, and even if they mingle with the common folk, they remain like gold and jade.

These were merely earth and stone. As for Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, their names have endured for ten thousand ages because they protected high positions and maintained the constant Way in their time, observing human nature and establishing laws according to its dispositions. Jie, Zhou, You, and Li, however, were deluded by wealth and honor.

One loses the great treasure and, though possessing its inherent nature, is carried away by emotional attachments. Although heaven and earth are devoid of emotion, the winds, clouds, and the four seasons alter their cycles;

the mountains, rivers, and myriad things disarray their forms. Only man dwells within them, measuring the timing of heaven and following the advantages of the earth without losing his seasonal rhythm.
Thus, man is the heart of heaven and earth. Emotion, will, and consciousness all originate from the fundamental nature.

These are merely external names for what is manifested according to the objects [they refer to]; the rest cannot be fully enumerated here. "Qing" (feeling) refers to the mind; it is drawn by its functions.
"Yi" (will/intention) refers to the resolve; it records matters. "Shi" (consciousness/cognition) refers to knowing; it discriminates objects. Love, hatred, joy, and anger are all *qing*.
As for those who are great sages, their nature is determined; they are not deluded by external things, nor are they... [influenced by them].
"Emotion binds; nature is constrained by emotion. This is why my teaching is called 'Perfect Enlightenment' (Samyak-saṃbodhi).
The *I Ching* only knows the doctrine of exhausting principles and perfecting nature, yet it has not yet seen the Way that transcends antiquity and enters the present."
In the autumn of the first year of the Shaosheng era, Su Hanzhi (Su Shi) passed through Nanhua.
Wearing a *nà* robe, he sat with the Elder Bian when a guest arrived to visit him; the guest was dressed in official robes.

Su then said to Bian, "To wear a *nà* robe on the inside and official robes on the outside is very much like 'suppressing the worthy to make way for the lowly. Bian replied, "If there were even a slight lack of external protection..."
Deshou said, "There is an echo within these words. Bian replied, "The entrustment at Vulture Peak must not be forgotten.
Shortly thereafter, he composed an inscription for the Sūchēng Hermitage. Its preface reads: "The hermitage of Master Chéng was built by the Elder Bian of Nanhua for my cousin Chéng Dérú.
When I passed it while migrating southward, I changed its name to Sūchēng and composed this inscription for it."
Bian built a hermitage south of Baolin; Cheng took it for himself, not out of greed. After Su arrived, there were three residents. Once Su had settled in, Cheng departed.
Within the snap of a finger, the three periods of time are complete. As I have said, such a thing has no basis in reality. A hundred thousand lamps share a single light;
within a single speck of dust, two sites of enlightenment preach the Dharma together without obstructing one another. Originally there is no penetration; how could there be any obstruction?
Cheng was not away; Su was not present. Each was fully pervasive, without confusion or impairment. Cheng served as the Commissioner of Grain for Guangdong, while Bian constructed this hermitage.
Master Xian first visited Master Gao’an Wugong at Yunju. Wugong asked, "Where is your native place? Xian replied, "Tiantai.
Wugong said, "The stone bridge at Tiantai has collapsed—is that so? Xian stepped forward and supported it with his hand; Wugong simply smiled.
In his daily life, Wugong delighted in citing the story of Xuansha addressing the assembly: "Because of me, you must pay homage. When Xian heard this, he...
Xing presented a verse to Wù, saying: "Because I bowed to you, my gills became like those of a fish and my beak like those of a bird;
if one asks further 'how,' ten thousand miles of white clouds. Not long after, he took his leave to return to his former home, where he maintained a high standard for himself.

Later, when Tōng’ān questioned Wù about him, Wù gave this report: "This matter must be practiced with vigor; after a long time, it will naturally manifest its spiritual efficacy. Previously, it was because of me that [he attained this]."

The "Eulogy for Paying Homage" may truly be said to have comprehended the past and surpassed the present. From that time on, his reputation for the Way spread in all directions, and he became an object of veneration for his era.
The Prefect changed the Wan’ian Vinaya Monastery into a Chan seat and appointed Xian as its founding abbot. Chan Master Xuedou Xingtang of Wujia regarded Xian as his own foster son.
While traveling at Tiantai, Xian requested him to ascend the seat [to give a formal discourse]. Xing composed a verse, which says: [Verse omitted per instructions]
"Because of me, you receive this prostration. Regarding the stone footbridge at Tiantai: of those who have come and gone through the ages, how many have personally trodden upon it?
He was naturally dignified and solemn; he was able to follow in the footsteps of Gaofeng An. Although he presided over several monasteries, he spent his final years at the Three Pagodas of Yunju.
Chan Master Fohui of Jiangshan, whom the monastic community called "Ten Thousand Volumes from the Spring," composed a poem titled *The Ballad of Beimaang* (*Beimang xing*), which says:
"The mountains before and behind are high and towering; Funeral carriages rattle past day after day. Mournful songs of deep resentment fill the crags and valleys;
Those who hear them secretly grieve at the *Xie-lu* chant. One cry of lamentation marks a parting for a thousand years; Filial sons and obedient grandsons shed tears of blood in vain."
What thing in this world can be deemed firm? The great ocean and Mount Sumeru shall eventually perish. Human life is like dew, easily withered;

from the beginning there has been meeting, but all ends in parting. Suffering, joy, grief, and lamentation do not cease for even a moment—how much more so when a hundred years pass as swiftly as a flash of lightning!
Those who depart drift away and never return. People today do not understand the intent of those of antiquity; they plant pine trees and set up stones.
Standing at the gates of the tombs, one seeks to provide for the long life of the deceased; yet their souls wander on, their forms transformed into earth.

The five realms of existence are vast and boundless, revolving like a well-wheel. Today’s people return to bury them in the graves of the ancients; these modern and ancient graves have no fixed owners.
Within the city of Luoyang are tens of millions of people, who in the end shall become dust beneath the North Mound Mountains. Immersed in delusion, they do not remember the path back home. For...
You sit alone, long consumed by grief and bitterness. In days past, you wept as you saw others off upon the long road; today, you lie by a solitary grave amidst the lush spring grass.
A sly fox burrows through the earth to shelter its young; a plowman turns up the bones in search of buried jewels. The withered trees sigh as wild winds arise;
ruined tombs stretch east and west toward the clear sky. The Cold Food Festival has already passed—whom do they now honor? Only the lingering flowers remain silent by the mound.
"Silent Red. The sun and moon hasten one another like flying arrows; whether poor or rich, wise or foolish, all are thus.

How can we attain the realm of eternal joy together, where even passing through the kalpa-fire there is neither birth nor death? Observing the sentiment and logic of these words, they are both poignant and grand, possessing a quality that pertains to edification.
Those in the world who harbor violent temperaments and are immersed in sensual pleasures should observe this and admonish themselves accordingly.
Ji, the administrative secretary of Xishu, resided at Baizhang Mountain for the longest period; he was thoroughly conversant with both Buddhist and secular classics.
As for his poetry and lyrics, although they are not refined or elegant, they contain many words of virtue. Master Guī had been a disciple of his from an early age;
he presented him with a poem that said: "In youth, your poetic meter was like spring rain, Drenching the myriad things to bring forth their finest qualities.
From time to time, a piece emerges with a fresh inspiration, Like patterned silk or light gauze, produced effortlessly from the loom. I know your literary meaning requires no further carving."

Day by day, artifice and falsehood increasingly obscure the heart-mind; suddenly turning away, one washes the mind to seek the Great Way. Transcending all, one does not consort with the myriad dharmas;
beneath Mount Chelun, follow me in my travels. Like bright white silk washed upon the autumn isles, once dyed it shines brilliantly with its true color, no longer ranked among the reds and purples.
On Mount Sumeru, nowhere is the cloud of virtue seen; within the dream-palaces...
Opening the lock of the door, the heart’s core is revealed clearly and cannot be obscured. There is no need for elaborate carving to obtain clever phrasing;

the Immortal of Exile resides within a single speck of dust, and within every speck of dust there is Du Fu. From the roots of consciousness to the realms of sensation, all are drafts stored within his belly—eighty-four thousand countless lines.
His meaning and phrasing are perfectly beautiful like a polished marble; one can never finish reciting them, and one longs to rise and dance. Autumn.
The wind circles the trees, sweeping away their verdant faces; the gardens lose their emerald hue, becoming like Mount Guliou. To pursue this pure inspiration, I bid farewell to my travels;

with a *lingran* (cool, ethereal) grace, I need not wait for the wind to serve as my charioteer. I summon this guest who has not yet returned for a hundred years; in the journeying forth, heaven and earth are but a single inn.
Desiring to gather the drops of spring rain to manifest new meaning, may we meet again on another day to raise a toast for you. Gui then departed and went to visit the Buddha.

He attained the Dharma through his eyes. Later, he resided at Baochan on Mount He, where he planted bamboo to the east of his quarters and established a secluded retreat there, naming it "Bamboo Hermitage.
He composed a poem: I have planted over a hundred bamboo stalks And built two or three thatched huts; They barely allow a path to the stream, Yet do not obstruct the mountains behind the house.
Yellow leaves drift with the water’s coming and going, White clouds pass back and forth with the wind. All my life has been nothing but this—this is the Way.
This person had few literary skills. The *Zhuan-an* (Bamboo Hut) was named Shigui; that it is recorded as Dao-gui in the *Shixuan* (Selection of Poetry) is an error.
*Yunwo Jitan*, Volume Lower (End). Written by the Abbot of Yunwo Monastery.

On the seventh day of the eleventh month, the Abbot of Yunwo Monastery at Ganshan in Qujiang, Fengcheng, Xiaoying, respectfully submits this memorial to inquire after the health of his venerable brother, Chan Master Wuyan of Dun’an at Mount Jing: "Recently, your brother resided at Shanglan."

I have now received your letter, which was delivered via the postal service. Having unfolded and read its true purport, my heart is deeply comforted—how much more so than one who, scorched by heat, bathes in a cool breeze!

However, as we are separated by a vast distance, it is extremely difficult to find leisure for correspondence; that I have been unable to submit even a brief report fills me with no small measure of shame and regret.
As the Tang poet Gu Kwang once said: "Twenty years have passed since our last parting; how many times can a person endure such farewells?"
The time since our parting has exceeded seven years, counting on my fingers; how can one endure this?

As I reflect back upon the benefits of our past cultivation of the Way and mutual refinement through righteousness, this heart of mine remains vividly clear, yet it feels as though we are separated by an entire lifetime.

I have humbly heard that you sit and distribute the gifts of the Dharma, awakening many people. Were it not for your pungent methods and great tongs and hammers, such a feat would not be easily achieved.
Therefore, I have once expressed my sentiments regarding this in the *geya* (verse) style, saying: "Jingshan rises abruptly above the clouds and mists;
Highly secluded at its peak, it severs all worldly ties. Grasping a black snake, he shares half his seat; Yet he turns his venomous breath toward humans and devas."
In truth, the ancestral hall’s profound trust rests upon this very point. I revere it, I revere it!

Now, as the middle month of winter arrives and the cold gradually intensifies, I am certain that you will experience physical well-being amidst the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), enjoying boundless joy in the merit of the constant veneration offered by the *nāgas* and devas.
As for myself, I consider my own fate to be meager and my talent sparse; taking but short steps on a narrow path, I find it difficult to keep pace with those who excel.

My friend’s lofty footsteps remain among the forest groves; yet, unable to avoid following my own resolve and fulfilling my lot, in the *xiánmǎo* year of the *qiándào* cycle, I constructed a hut on a desolate mountain.

As it was high, cold, isolated, and remote, I could no longer endure my old age and illness. Consequently, in the winter of the *wùxū* year of the *chúnxī* cycle, I registered my disciples at the small temple of Gānshān and moved my residence there.
The temple grounds required thirty-one *qián* in tax, and there were no permanent endowments.
His dwelling consisted of only a few dilapidated rooms, much like the residence of Yutianzi in the city of Luoyang.

His relatives and old friends, pitying his poor means of livelihood and his austere lifestyle, pooled their resources to establish a small *dharmacakra* (wheel-treasury) for him, hoping that both wealth and Dharma might be presented there to supplement his daily sustenance.
In the year of Kaimao, his disciple suddenly passed away, whereupon he himself took charge of the sweeping and maintenance.
He was conscientious; beyond measuring the firewood and counting the grains of rice, he harbored no other thoughts in his breast, seeking only the comfort of sleep.
When his elder brother Yin retired from affairs at Shanglan, [Dongshan] went to the mountains and, finding joy in their secluded stillness, remained there for eleven months.
At the invitation of Nanyuan, he moved to the ancestral seat of Qingyuan, where his Dharma influence flourished greatly, and there were also two or three monks [under him].
My son, do not let the bamboo rattle remain unused. This bamboo rattle was used by my late teacher, Dahui, while he was at Mei Yang;

when he came to Bao’en Temple, it was for the sake of his dharma brothers who had entered the inner room. Wuzhuo once composed an inscription to record its origins. The preface to the inscription states:
"The late teacher Dahui employed the bamboo rattle to reveal the wondrous essence that has not been transmitted by the Buddhas and patriarchs for nearly forty years."
Thus, the orthodox lineage of Linji was made to flourish. Even while dwelling in the midst of hardship, he never grew weary of wielding the staff and striking;
hence, the bamboo rattle remained in the Hall Office at Baen Monastery in Meizhou. Ying Zhongwen of Jiangxi once held this office and brought it back with him.
Is this not a source of glory for the monastic community for a thousand years? Wuzhuo Miao...
In total reverence, I bow my head and compose this inscription: On the Southern Mountain there is bamboo; it is naturally distinct without being pared.

Its form is like that of a black viper, emitting a hissing, poisonous breath. Like a staff a cubit long, its use is inexhaustible. It forges the sages and boils the common folk, weaving through heaven and across the earth.
Zhongwen obtained it; he should especially keep it secret so that it may illuminate the monastic community and not fall into ruin for a thousand ages.

I, a foolish fellow, am sinking into the common world, yet having acquired this, it truly becomes a piece of idle furniture. After my death, it will surely be taken by the likes of Mānava to stir the embers.
How wonderful it would be if, before the coffin is closed, the bamboo comb and the inscription personally written by Wuzhu were both returned to you, my brother Yin.
It is fortunate that these items have proven efficacious; I imagine you will surely rejoice upon hearing of this.
Among the brothers at Mount Tou, none had a bond with you as deep as yours, and after crossing the Jiangxi, the only one I have been able to see again is Guogang.
Brother Yong was commissioned by Yangshan to travel via Fengcheng to visit me at my hermitage.
After escorting him into the monastery, he later moved to Daguai, where he passed away after two years. Brother Huì of Changxi resided at Xiangcheng and also came to my mountain dwelling;
while serving as the abbot of Daguai, he passed away after one month. Brother Yuan of Jianchang moved from Ehu...
Yangshan traveled by circuitous routes to seek him out, escorting him as far as Huili Temple on the banks of the River Linjiang.

Not long after, he took charge of the temple affairs for seven days before departing for the west. Thus, the karmic conditions of his two elder brothers, Hui and Yuan, were not granted to them; such was their lot.
What cause for regret could there be? Master Yuyang was your elder brother; such was the abundance of his spiritual merit.

Previously, while we traveled together by day and dwelt together by night, many did not recognize that the Venerable Wei was a person of such noble status. Since he entered the world of transcendence, you have collected three or four of his writings.

As he once resided at Lingyin, I previously inquired of him regarding these writings, saying: "Brother, you have now transformed your ordinary mortal bones into those of a soaring immortal. You have raised [this] from its former state..."
When fish become clouds and dragons, there are those such as your elder brothers Yan and Yuan, yet they have not yet heard of themselves being "pushed forward" by humans and devas. Why is this?
Although your elder brothers do not rely on the remaining arguments from their teeth and jaws, the fragrance of their Way and the wind of their virtue naturally spread and manifest.
The reason for my inquiry is that I hope you will not forget to uphold the public consensus of the monastic communities throughout the world. Now, within these communities...

There is no public consensus. What can be done? What can be done? Last summer, my elder brother Mì of Jingci sent me a letter, expressing his sincerity and utmost devotion, never abandoning the ancestral Way of old.
We were truly relying on him to preside over the community as the one to whom authentic *zhai-zi* (monastics) would turn.
Who would have thought that last summer he would suddenly cross the Pamir Mountains and depart? My brother must surely be disheartened by this. Moreover, among our friends throughout the Jianghu...
The old [manuscripts] have withered and fallen away like frost-touched leaves shed from trees; there remain but few, which truly causes one to feel deep sorrow.
Now my elder brother Lian of Huazang resides at Baoguan and sends me a letter daily, stating that Ancestral Master Yong has lived at Xingshan in Yue for several years.
While in Lin’an, he compiled the life and deeds of Dahui, producing a single volume of an annual chronology (nianpu), yet he was unwilling to submit it to the Imperial Library.
